Every design run and the probe pass, and every written, twin and reach run ends on the one invariant its configuration names. The design runs and the probe used four workers and the others two, on a machine four build lanes were loading, at a load average between 95 and 165 on 14 cores; the times are several times what the same runs take on an idle one. With more than one worker a trace is the first one TLC's workers met, which may be a state or two longer than the shortest, and a twin's count is what TLC had explored when it met the violation. The largest run held 406 MB on disk. A first form of `DropJob`, with a paused attempt beside its stalled write, was stopped at 4.9 M distinct states and a growing queue after 5 min, to spare the machine; `DropJob` and the probe then ran without the pause, which `DropJob-Cite` and `DropJob-Adopt` keep, each for its own kinds.

What the runs cover: every interleaving, at those bounds, of the DROP's commit, two pushes of any of the three kinds on the refs their kind allows, a head write that stalls holding its key and lands or reverts at any later time, a process paused before its head write, the evacuator's resolve and fence at any time its minute allows, and the job's phases and rounds. The stalled first commit to a ref with no head is in every design run: `DropJobReach-LateCreation` shows a first commit to that ref naming the candidate beside a running job, and `DropJobReach-Keeps` the job ending with the candidate kept for a version that came to name it. Each finding of 10.1 E and F appears against the text as written or with its rule broken, and is gone in the design: E1 in `DropJobWritten-NewRef`, E2 in `DropJobWritten-CachedHead`, E3 in `DropJobWritten-YoungAdopter`, F in `DropJobTwin-CandidatesBySweep` and `DropJobTwin-MarkSkipsHistory`, and the order of F4 before F5 and F6 in `DropJobTwin-HorizonAfterScans`. `DropJobProbe-ScanPastHeldKey` passes with the scans reading past a held key: the horizon has already waited for every record a held write can belong to, so the scans' wait on a held key is the store's behavior and no fence of the job's.

What they do not hold. The model's lists are exact and its lineage one path on one ref: resolve's link and set checks, and L1 to L4, are arguments above and tests in 10.6. The fence is abstract, a citation passing until the DROP is visible to it: 5h's window and mark rows, the removed boundary's mark among them, are 10.2.7's rules and 10.6's tests. One job instance runs: a second instance's late DELETE is section 2's D, checked in `EvsGc.tla` for a DELETE that names its object, which F9 uses. The window, the cancel, the lock, holds and the lease stay `EvsCommit.tla`'s drop stories. The cache stamp is the arithmetic of 10.2.7, and the model takes its conclusion, a cached head that hides the DROP for a bounded time.

### 10.4 Cost

Against §11.9's 4 MiB a catch-up, §11.13's 32 MB/s of reads and 10 deletes a second a job, and §11.8's three round trips a push.

```text
a head reader, one drop       at most 263,312 B (257.1 KiB) once: 6.3% of the budget; typical 1.4 KiB (one lineage,
                              depth 8, one epoch). Every later read under that drop: nothing (held_drops)
  its checking                one SHA-256 over the body (256 KiB at a phone's 100 to 250 MB/s: 1 to 3 ms), one
                              signature, and E x d HMAC-SHA256 for H5 (300 epochs at depth 8: 2,400, about 2 ms);
                              one EvsDropPath in memory at a time; the body on storage, 4 MiB of them a network
  a reply                     at most 1 MiB of bodies; a 64-path read under 64 different drops takes further
                              reads, 4 bodies or more each
a body                        depth 8, 1 epoch: 195 B a lineage, 1,024 of them 198 KiB, one push
                              depth 16, 1 epoch: 339 B; 766 a push       depth 32, 1 epoch: 627 B; 416 a push
                              depth 8, 4 epochs: 650 B; 401 a push       depth 32, 4 epochs: 2,378 B; 110 a push
                              depth 8, 100 epochs: 14.8 KiB; 17 a push   depth 8, 300 epochs: 44.5 KiB; 5 a push
                              one lineage passes the bound at 1,725 epochs at depth 8, 449 at depth 32
lists                         32 B a version: 3.1 MiB for 100,000 versions (4 parts), 32 MiB at the bound (33
                              parts beside the changes', 51 at most). evs's seal streams them: one value and one
                              hash held. They stay in the push's records for the ref's life, as any payload does
a head-mode signer            one statement, and an entry version, per version walked: 4 MiB for about 4,000 to
                              8,000 versions, then refused in favor of a mirroring device
the push path                 unchanged: no read, write or round added. 5h reads bit-5 bodies as QD-389 has it,
                              each at most 256 KiB, cached. The cache stamp costs nothing
a push in parts               a part's record carries each replaced version's ids whole, at most 2,048; the seal
                              makes the list from parts it reads already: no entry is read twice
resolve                       one pass over the DROP's ref: its log pages and each matching push's record. A ref
                              of 10 M versions at 2 KiB a record is 20 GiB: 11 min 11 s at 32 MB/s. One map part,
                              at most 8 MiB, per lineage link, shared by lineages whose moves sit in one part
mark, verify                  each one pass over every ref's records: 1 M versions at 2 KiB, 2 GiB, 67 s; 100 M,
                              200 GiB, 1 h 52 min; twice. A later round reads only what committed since
deletes                       a HEAD and a DELETE an id, 10 a second: 1 M segments in 27 h 47 min, on the HDDs,
                              spending no NVMe budget; a slot's DELETE ~3.5 KiB a drive
the listed index              35 B a row, an index of 32 B per 128 rows and a bloom of 10 bits a row: 36.5 B a
                              listed version, 36.5 MiB at 2^20, on the segment cluster for the repo's life. Not
                              in any network's stored bytes, as dropscan/ is not today
evs, a repo with no drop      one GET of drops/<repo>/_ answering 404, cached 5 s, on reads of older versions and
                              of records holding an inline record; nothing on a head read
evs, a repo with drops        parsed bodies and each list file's index and bloom in memory (1.5 MiB per 2^20
                              rows), within 64 MiB a process; one LIST of dropscan/<repo>/ each 10 min; one 4,480 B
                              range read on the segment cluster per bloom hit, 1% of the versions not listed
the table                     one CAS a phase and at most one a minute, 14 to 22 KiB a drive each, as §11.13 has
a `now` drop                  its deletes start 25 h 12 min to 26 h 12 min after it, where owner decision 204
                              says about 25 to 26 h; a candidate uploaded under 49 h before a round waits for its
                              bound, at most 49 h 2 min from its upload plus the hour to evacuation's next run
a 7-day drop                  no wait beyond owner decision 183's 25 min: both bounds are days past. It is never
                              covered by a job that waits for a `now` drop's bound (10.2.8), but a drop whose start
                              passes while such a job waits or deletes starts after it, as under one job a repo
```

No budget of §11.9 or §11.13 is passed. Two things grow and are the owner's to accept (10.9): a `now` drop of content under two days old holds that content up to a day longer, and the listed index stays for the repo's life.

### 10.5 Failure modes and recovery

```text
the job killed anywhere        another instance takes it by If-Match once the lease lapsed 30 s ago (§11.13's who
                               row) and resumes from the job record: resolve runs again whole and writes equal
                               files (a 412 on equal bytes is success); a round killed before its verify ended
                               restarts at its F4, reading the horizon again, with marks kept; one killed in its
                               deletes resumes at the cursor under that round's horizon, which its scans followed
a stale instance wakes         its table CAS fails and it stops. A DELETE it had issued carries its lease's
                               deadline and its HEAD's LastModified: the store refuses it past the deadline, and it
                               takes the object that instance judged or nothing (F9)
evacuation falls behind        the horizon stops, F4 does not open and young ids stay young: the job sits in phase
                               horizon, deleting nothing, and reads as executing. §19.8's oldest-batch age alarms
                               past 26 h. The job retries each 10 min once its retry_ms passed
a head write stalls on a       its key is held; evacuation's read or fence of it waits and the horizon with it
record's ref                   (2.5), so the job waits. §19.8 pages a key held over 1 min. The write lands and the
                               scans read it, or it is reverted and its record dies
a first commit to a new ref    the same: evacuation's placeholder waits behind the held key. Landed: the ref has a
stalls across the job          head when the round lists head/, and its version marks what it names. Reverted: the
                               placeholder fences the ref and the record is dead
a head held during a scan      the read answers 503; the phase waits and retries. A scan never skips a ref
a LIST not whole               503 from the store (2.2.2; QD-663 for a key mid-overwrite): the horizon's LIST or
                               the LIST of head/ fails and the phase waits
SettlePassed false, or the     F0: no phase advances and nothing is deleted (§19.6)
clock unsure
a list or link off the         refused {mismatch} at resolve, before any file a reader uses: a void record, a page
history                        naming how many values the list lacks and adds; nothing deleted, content served
the scans disagree             refused {verify}: a page; nothing deleted in that round or after. Ids an earlier
                               round deleted passed that round's two scans and stay deleted
a version names a candidate    marked and kept; urnetwork_evs_drop_late_marks_total counts it. For an id whose
after M                        bound the horizon had passed, that is a broken fence: §19.8 alarms on any count
                               there (drop_late_mark), and the id stays
a hold placed mid-job          F8: the rest of D moves to held; the drop reads done; a round over the held ids
                               runs when every covering hold ends (owner decision 184)
a lock filed after the start   verify's reread refuses the job {locked} before a round's first DELETE (§11.13's
                               verify row); a round already deleting finishes its batch
the DropSink append lost       the drop is not in the table: nothing starts. A read or push that meets its bit-5
                               window entry appends it, as evacuation does within 26 h; seen_ms is then later
                               than it need be, which only delays a `now` drop
the cache put fails or         a stale head is served until 10 min past its own written_ms, whenever it was put:
comes late                     C1's bound
a body or lists past the       the client cuts the drop into several pushes, each previewed; one lineage alone
bounds                         past a bound: ErrEvsDropTooLarge, nothing sent. evs refuses a longer body 400
                               INVALID and more values 409 DROP_LIST
a seal with a part missing     409 PARTS_MISSING, as any push; a DROP's body and lists are checked only by a seal
                               that holds every part
a reader's body check fails    10.2.3's verdict table: tampering, invalid, or evs's state ignored
a reader lacks a body it       drop_body empty past 1 MiB of bodies in the reply: it reads the path again
needs
a list file unreadable         evs answers the read 503: it does not serve a version it cannot clear of a drop
(503, a bad trailer)           while the repo has drops. A bad trailer alarms drop_index_corrupt, which pages; the
                               file is deleted and written again, equal bytes, by running resolve again for its
                               job's drops, from their bodies and the ref's history (an operations command, 10.7)
a re-seed from a stale         §19.10's re-seeded job runs again from its signed state (FI-27's last clause):
mirror                         resolve rewrites the list files, equal bytes, and the rounds delete what returned
```

### 10.7 Implementation notes, task by task

One new task carries the format changes and the changes to landed code that no held task owns. It goes first, so the held ones can name it. The proposal, in the plan's format, is `.stack/plan/proposals/details-10-tasks.md`.

**New: EVS2-M10-36, section 10's formats and the landed codecs** (sidecar; M; before every task below). `protocol/evs.proto` and `evs.pb.go`: 10.2.2's four additions. `protocol/EVS-FORMAT.md`: the DROP chapter takes 10.2.2's rules (body bound, total count, section 9 in part 1, the empty change list for a changeless DROP), the membership paragraph takes 10.2.3's `Covers` and what a reply carries, the drop routes' table takes `map_parts` and `linked`, the purge chapter takes the `replaced` flag, and both items under "Not fixed here" that name questions evs2-m10-03 and evs2-m10-04 go. `testdata/evs/format2/schema.yml` and `metadata_rows.yml`: the new fields, each on the row 10.8 names. `evs_drop_payload.go`: `EvsDropMaxBodyByteCount`, checked in `evsCheckDropBody` before the hash; `evsDropListChecker` sums the counts and refuses past `EvsDropMaxListedCount` with `ErrEvsDropList`; `ErrEvsDropTooLarge`. `evs_statement.go`: `buildParts` lays a DROP out as 10.2.5 (section 9 whole in part 1, values never split, `DropListPartValueCount` a changeless part, the empty change list when there is no change); `evs_payload.go`: a DROP in parts whose section 9 is not whole in part 1 is INVALID, and an `EvsPurgeList` with `replaced` in a push's or seal's tail is INVALID. `evsservice/head_cache.go`: `HeadCache.Write` stamps `cachedMs` from the committed head's `written_ms`, bounded above by the clock (10.2.7). `evsservice/fold_format2.go` and `entry.go`: the fold of a DROP sets a removed boundary's drop mark on its marker's entry (10.2.7's removed row), `dropMarksAt` no longer skipping boundary 2, and `ParseEvsIndexEntry` takes a mark equal to its marker's path version. `evsservice/sweep.go`: the hold-end and turn-on passes and evacuation's sweep take candidates from push and seal records and skip a list with `replaced` set, where today the pass sweeps "each of its parts', since a part lists what it replaced" (`sweep.go:580-601`); `sweep_recompute.go` keeps reading every part's versions for a marked seal. Tests: 10.6's `evs_drop_payload_test.go`, `evs_statement_test.go`, `head_test.go`, `sweep_test.go` and `fold_format2_test.go` rows, and the vectors. Traps: the body bound is checked on the received length before any hashing, on evs and on a reader; a part's `replaced` list is never a candidate list, whoever reads it; the stamp must not be later than the clock, or a head with a wrong `written_ms` would be served longer.

**EVS2-M10-09, the DROP push on evs** (held; L; scope grows by the seal's DROP checks, `seen_ms` and the fence's exact rule). Build its plan entry with these changes. `check_drop.go`: 5c's body-free DROP rules at a part and its body rules at the seal or the one-part step 5 (10.2.5's two rows); `evs_drops_per_day` is counted once, at the seal. `push_seal.go`: section 9 from part 1, `EvsCheckDropPayload` streaming section 10's slices, the boundary rules per lineage against the parts' changes, the base's hash looked for in its path's values as they stream. `check_dropped.go`: 10.2.7's window, mark and seal rows; the bit-5 bodies come from `push_step4.go`'s round (a DROP in parts: its part 1), cached per process by (ref, version). `push_drop.go`: `DropSink.Append` takes the drop's table entry as 10.2.2 lays it out (for a cancel, the drop it ends and its version) with `seen_ms`, the clock read after step 7's 200, and nothing is appended on an unsure clock; a push or read that meets a bit-5 window entry the table lacks calls it again with a clock read after the cluster read that showed the entry. A removed boundary whose newest lineage entry is in an epoch that is neither current nor a listed source has no entry to check at the push: evs checks its shape alone and leaves the boundary to resolve. Needs gain EVS2-M10-36. Traps: no DROP check that needs the body runs at a part; a cancelled or refused drop still fences; the fence refuses on a cluster read only (the refuse row), so a cached head that shows the DROP sends 5h to the cluster before it answers. Tests: 10.6's `push_parts_test.go`, `check_dropped_test.go` and `drop_table_test.go` rows beside its plan entry's.

**EVS2-M10-10, serving listed versions** (held; M; scope changes: the lookup is 10.2.9's, and the list files are read here). `read_drop.go`: `DropOf` and `state`. `drop_index.go` (new): a per-process `DropIndex` holding, per repo with a `drops/<repo>/_`, the parsed bodies of its live drops and each list file's index and bloom, within `DropIndexByteCount`; one LIST of `dropscan/<repo>/` each `DropIndexRefresh`. The reply's `drop_statement` and `drop_body` once per drop, bodies up to `DropBodyReplyByteCount`, none for a version in `held_drops`. `read_elide.go`: 10.2.9's entry and records rows; zeros of the same length, never a shorter frame. `read_withheld.go` stays as planned (the del and held files through the table). Membership no longer needs the path's entry or its drop mark; do not read `idx/` for it. Its Needs gain EVS2-M10-36 and EVSB-M10-04's list files in place of "question plan-EVS2-drop-list-proof". Traps: a read fails 503 rather than serve a version it could not clear while a list file is unreadable; a void record outranks a row; a sealed hold's answers stay byte-equal to a no-hold twin's, so nothing here reads `hold/`; evs's clock decides `drop_pending` against `dropped` on the wire and the reader's own decides what it shows. Tests: 10.6's `read_drop_test.go` and `read_elide_test.go` rows beside its plan entry's.

**EVS2-M10-22, drops on readers** (held; M; scope fixed by 10.2.3). `evs_drop_verify.go`: H0 to H7 and the verdict table, with the replaying reader's exactness check computed from its own history, no list fetched. `evs_drop_state.go`: `EvsDropState`, the sealed store of checked bodies by (repo, ref, drop version) within `DropBodyKeepByteCount`, `held_drops` on each read, and a second read when a body was left out. `evs_drop_apply.go`: an executed drop is applied by `Covers` over what the device holds: for each version it keeps content of, by (epoch, token path, version), under each drop whose window passed with no cancel and no refused report; it hands `Sidecar.ApplyExecutedDrop` the ids only such versions name, as planned. A body is streamed to storage and parsed one path at a time (QD-641). Its Needs gain EVS2-M10-36. Traps: the name and the version judged are the reader's own, never a field of the reply; a lineage entry in an epoch the device holds no key for cannot occur for a reader of the current epoch, and is treated as H5 failing; a zeroed entry version under a dropped path is no alarm, and one under any other path is. Tests: 10.6's `evs_drop_verify_test.go` and `evs_drop_state_test.go` rows beside its plan entry's.

**EVSB-M10-03, drop table, job lifecycle and dry runs** (held; L; scope grows by the horizon phase and the dry run's links). `drop_table.go`: the entry's `seen_ms` and the job record's `round`, `fence_ms`, `horizon_ms` and `retry_ms` (10.2.2); `DropSink.Append(drop, seenMs)`; evacuation's append and the repair append set `seen_ms` after their own cluster read. `drop_job.go`: 10.2.8's transition table and F0 to F9 in order; `start` as written there; phase horizon releases the lease and sets `retry_ms`, and taskworker's schedule (`server/taskworker/evs_drop.go`) wakes the job at `retry_ms` and then each 10 min; `OrphanHorizon` is EVSB-M2-12's (`nightly.go`), called before the LIST of `head/` in every round. `drop_routes.go`: the dry run runs resolve's link and set checks at a snapshot and answers each path's `map_parts` and `linked` beside `list_match`; `young_bytes` counts candidates whose LastModified + `AdoptionBound` is past the snapshot's horizon. `EvsDropStatus.phase` reports `EVS_DROP_HORIZON` while the job waits. Barriers as 10.6's `drop_job_test.go` row names them. Its Needs gain EVS2-M10-36 and EVSB-M2-12's `OrphanHorizon`. Traps: the horizon is read anew at the start of every round, and again when a restart redoes a round's scans, and F4 never takes it from the job record, which keeps it for that round's F7 alone; a job that waits holds no lease; the 25 min of `DropStartDelay` stays, since owner decision 183 states it and a cancel's last minute rests on it; `seen_ms` is never earlier than the answer that showed the commit. Tests: 10.6's `drop_table_test.go` and `drop_job_test.go` rows beside its plan entry's; FS-89's `--now` clause on the fake clock at 25 h, 25 h 12 min and 26 h 12 min.

**EVSB-M10-04, drop resolve and mark** (held; L; scope changes: resolve enumerates by a scan and writes the list files; mark's `Names`). `drop_resolve.go`: 10.2.8's `resolve`, each covered drop judged alone; exactness by count and hash, section 10 read only to describe a mismatch; a removal of a directory holding the path counts as the path's removal; candidates from S's kind-1 locators and slot ids and from nothing else, with no LIST of `seg/` anywhere in the package (G11); the list files of 10.2.9, written before the cand file. `drop_mark.go`: the LIST of `head/` after the round's horizon, each head from the cluster with a held key waited out, `Names` with a git-mode push's new-objects list, liveness by the list files (a version whose entry hash a row lists under a drop that is covered and not refused, or executed, marks nothing), marks appended with the cursor. A dry run's marks stand as planned. Its Needs gain EVS2-M10-36. Traps: resolve runs again whole after a kill and must write byte-equal files; a ref's mode comes from its head, and a placeholder head has no version to scan; marks never shrink; the scan compares ids and decrypts nothing. Tests: 10.6's `drop_resolve_test.go` and `drop_mark_test.go` rows; FS-93; FS-91 (a) to (f) on mark's side. A corrupt list file is rebuilt by running resolve again for its job's drops after deleting it, which is an operations command (`sidecarctl evs drop-reindex <repo>`): the ops lane owns `sidecarctl`, so this task raises it and ships the function it calls.

**Other tasks this section touches by name.**

### 10.8 Proposed DESIGN.md text

For a design-records track. Each item replaces the words it quotes and leaves the rest of its row.

**§11.6, `EvsDropHistory` and `EvsDropPath`.** `paths`' comment: "drop: 1 to 1,024 lineages, sorted by their newest token path's bytes; the body at most 256 KiB as bytes". `count`'s: "listed versions, 1 to 1,048,576, and at most that many over all of a DROP's paths". `listed_sha256`'s: "SHA-256 over the listed entry_sha256 values, ascending, which follow the body in the payload, spread over the push's parts past one part's 1 MiB; a check of the signer's enumeration, which the job's resolve and a replaying reader recompute and no reader is sent". The payload row, for "a DROP's EvsDropHistory and then its sorted lists, across the push's parts when large (11.7)": "a DROP's EvsDropHistory, whole in part 1, and then its sorted lists, across the push's parts when large, in parts that hold no change once the changes end (11.7, 11.8's parts row)". The checks row, after "sorted and unrepeated (409 DROP_LIST)": ", a DROP's body within 256 KiB and its counts within 1,048,576 in all".

**§11.7, the action row.** For "and marks only once evacuation's horizon has passed the drop's commit by 2 min, so a now drop's deletions start about 25 to 26 h after it (owner decision 204)": "and marks only once evacuation's horizon has passed, by 12 min, the time evs saw the drop committed, which covers a citation validated on a cached head, so a now drop's deletions start about 25 to 26 h after it (owner decision 204), and it deletes an object only once the horizon has passed its LastModified + 24 h + 2 min". ### 10.9 Owner questions

This section is designed on the recommendation of each.

1. **Does a head reader decide from the body alone** (`details-10-list-commitment.md`)? QD-153 said yes; this problem's brief asked for a commitment that supports range proofs, or the argument that the body suffices. Options: (1) the body alone, `listed_sha256` a flat hash, the body bounded (10.2.3): no format change, no proof, 257.1 KiB at most a drop and typically 1.4 KiB; (2) `listed_sha256` becomes an RFC 9162 root over the listed values and a reply carries an inclusion path, at most 20 hashes, 640 B, or a range of j leaves with at most 40 hashes beside them: a head reader then learns that the signer listed this very entry hash, which matters only for a DROP whose list disagrees with its own body, a DROP that never executes; evs must find a leaf's position among up to 2^20 values spread over 33 parts for every such read, or keep the tree; a format change and a prover and verifier on every leg; (3) both, the proof optional. **Recommendation: (1).** L1 to L3 show the body decides exactly what an executing drop lists, and the reader still needs the body with a proof, to tie the drop to the name.

2. **A bound on a DROP's body and on its lists** (`details-10-drop-bounds.md`). Options: (1) the body at most 256 KiB and the counts at most 2^20 in all, a larger drop cut into several pushes by the client: a `--recursive` drop of 1,024 files in a repository 300 path epochs old takes about 200 pushes of 5 lineages, each counted by `evs_drops_per_day`; (2) no body bound, and a Merkle root over the paths so a reader fetches one lineage and its proof: a second commitment and a split body, for a lineage that may itself be 44 KiB; (3) no bound: a phone may be sent a 44 MiB body. **Recommendation: (1)**, and that `evs_drops_per_day` count a command's pushes as one drop if (1)'s arithmetic ever bites, which D-QUOTA-12's owner can decide then.

3. **The job's margin past a drop's commit** (`details-10-cite-bound.md`). QD-626 says 2 min. FS-91 (c) has a citation validated on a cached head up to 10 min after the commit, and a creating push among those is E1 again. Options: (1) 12 min past the time evs saw the commit, and the cache stamped with the head's own write time so a late put cannot stretch it: a `now` drop's deletes start 10 min later than QD-626 has them, and two lines change in the landed cache; (2) keep 2 min and have step 4 read every reuse source's ref head from the cluster: one more read, 13 to 27 ms, on every push that copies across refs, and FS-91 (c) goes; (3) keep 2 min as decided and accept the hole. **Recommendation: (1).**

4. **Young by the horizon** (`details-10-young-horizon.md`). §11.13, I-EVS-15 and FI-27 delete a candidate "over 25 h old"; E3 shows that is section 2's finding A again. Options: (1) a candidate goes only once the horizon has passed its LastModified + 24 h + 2 min, as orphan GC's rule has it: nothing changes for a 7-day drop, and a `now` drop of content uploaded within two days keeps it until about 49 h after its upload; (2) keep 25 h and accept that an adopter creating its ref can lose its segment; (3) keep 25 h and refuse a receipt for any id in an executing job's candidates: evs's upload route then reads job files, and a race remains between a receipt and the job's start. **Recommendation: (1).**

5. **The listed index, for the repo's life** (`details-10-listed-index.md`). Options: (1) resolve writes each job's listed entry hashes to `dropscan/`, kept for the repo's life, and evs finds a listed version by its entry hash (10.2.9): 36.5 B a listed version on the HDDs, a changed lifetime in §11.8's `dropscan/` row and evs-28, and the drop mark left to the fence; (2) drop marks everywhere: a mark for a removed boundary, markers that carry a mark never collected, a new key under `idx/` for a mark whose epoch drains, a chain of earlier marks for a path dropped twice, and still no way to elide an inline record read by push id in an old epoch: changes to the landed fold, collection and copy; (3) accept that a dropped version of a removed path reads as a missing segment after 30 d and that its inline bytes are served again. **Recommendation: (1).** (3) returns content a drop was signed to hide.

6. **A phone that signs a drop** (`details-10-head-signer.md`). Options: (1) a head-mode device builds its list by walking the path's versions itself, within 4 MiB, and refuses a longer history in favor of a mirroring device; (2) the dry run returns the list and the phone signs it: any size works, and the list then says nothing its signer saw, so resolve's cross-check is evs checking itself; (3) §18.5's `DropHistory` leaves the SDK. **Recommendation: (1).**

**Questions this section answers.** `plan-EVS2-drop-list-proof`: its option 1, as QD-153 decided, with the body bounded and the reader's check made exact. `evs2-m10-03-drop-list-parts-without-changes`: its option 1, which QD-601 and QD-658 have since made the rule for every push; 10.2.5 is the DROP's layout under it. `evs2-m10-04-purge-across-parts`: its option 1, the part's record carrying what it replaced so the seal reads no entry again. `evs2-m10-01-metadata-rows`: its option 1, with this section's fields added to the same two rows (10.8). `plan-EVS2-drop-list-parts` (QD-167), `plan-EVS2-drop-table-bound` (QD-179), `plan-EVS2-drop-path-visibility` (QD-198) and `plan-EVS2-small-readings` stand as decided; QD-179's entry gains `seen_ms` within its 128 B. `evs1-m2-41-list-drops-overwritten-key` (QD-663) is relied on for the job's LIST of `head/`, as 2.2.2's whole LIST is. One reading is taken without a question: §11.7's index-entries row promises a drop mark "per dropped path", its fold row and the landed fold give one only where a DROP writes, and 10.2.7 gives a removed boundary its mark, without which its fence ends when the DROP leaves the window.

## 11. Canonical text extraction and exact body sizes for search

Status: complete (2026-11-10; amended 2026-11-12, QD-760: 11.2.1, 11.2.3, 11.2.7, 11.4, 11.5, 11.6, 11.7 and 11.8, each place marked)

Tasks held until complete: SEARCH-M10-31, SEARCH-M10-36.

Vectors: `sidecar/testdata/index/conformance/` (`mail.json`, `file.json`, `entities.json`, `charsets.json`, `sizes.json`). New tasks: `.stack/plan/proposals/details-11-tasks.md` (SEARCH-M10-42, SEARCH-M10-43, SEARCH-M10-44). Questions filed: `.stack/questions/details-11-own-decoders.md`, `details-11-extraction-bounds.md`, `details-11-body-encoding.md`, `details-11-small-readings.md`, `details-11-mail-snippet-reading.md`. Questions this section answers, each as 11.9 says: `search-m10-05-extractor-unstated-bytes`, `search-m10-07-extractor-field-placement`, and `plan-SEARCH-exact-body-sizes` as the owner decided it (QD-215). It amends one proposed fill, QD-474, in three places that 11.9 names.

### 11.1 The problem

Two things in §11.14 must come out byte for byte the same on every device, and neither is written down far enough to build.

**Extraction.** An index entry is a document's row and its key set, and a key set is the trigrams of the document's normalized text. A device that holds a document's text rebuilds the entry and compares it with what the writer committed, and raises `index_mismatch` naming the signer when they differ (§11.14's coverage and reproduce rows; FI-22). So every byte the extractor hands the normalizer is a format byte. §11.14's extract row gives mail three lines, and `protocol/INDEX-FORMAT.md`'s Extractor 1 a dozen. Two implementations were written apart from them, as D-TEST-14 asks: `indexExtractMail` (SEARCH-M10-06) and SearchOracle's extractor (SEARCH-M10-07). Four things are wrong or missing.

*A. The two disagree.* On honest mail they agree. On the inputs below, each a vector in `mail.json`, they do not, and each difference changes the key set:

```text
vector                         input                                      index            oracle
x-script-end-name              a<script>x</scriptx>y</script>z            az               ayz
t-base64-nbsp-stops            base64 body  SGVs U+00A0 bG8=              Hel              Hello
w-charset-with-space           Subject: =?UTF 8?Q?a?=                     as written       a
w-nbsp-between, w-cr-between   =?UTF-8?Q?a?= U+00A0 =?UTF-8?Q?b?=         a U+00A0 b       ab
p-sections-without-zero        filename=plain.txt; filename*1=b           plain.txt        (empty)
p-sections-empty-fall-through  filename*0=""; filename=plain.txt          plain.txt        (empty)
p-sections-repeat              filename*0=a; filename*0=b                 a                b
b-unterminated                 a multipart with no close delimiter,       two CR LF        two
                               whose last part is  two CR LF
```

The first, second, third and fifth are the ones question search-m10-05-extractor-unstated-bytes lists. The other four were found here, by running both over the vectors. To look for more, a copy of the oracle was made to read as the index does at exactly these six places (the script end tag, the bytes base64 skips, a word's charset, what counts as space between two words, RFC 2231's sections and precedence, the last part's line break) and fuzzed against the index: 2,263,165 executions in two runs, seeded with the vectors, found no other difference.

*B. Where they agree, they agree because both call the same library, and what those calls do on malformed input is written nowhere.* Each of these is what Go 1.27.3 does today, shown by a vector, and none is a rule of the format:

```text
t-qp-long-line        mime/quotedprintable reads lines through a 4,096 B buffer: a quoted-printable part with one
                      longer line loses everything after that line's first 4,096 B. Both extractors lose it.
t-qp-control-bytes    the same reader stops at a NUL, an ESC or a DEL: the rest of the part is lost
t-base64-unpadded     encoding/base64 gives nothing for a last group without its padding: a body that is cut, or
                      whose writer left the padding off, loses its last one or two bytes
e-one-digit           html.UnescapeString leaves "&#9 x" as it is, and decodes "&#9;x" and "&#65 x"
e-no-digits           it reads "&#x;" as U+FFFD
e-overflow            it adds digits in 32 bits: "&#4294967361;" is "A"
e-two-code-points     it has 2,229 of HTML's 2,231 names: "&nLt;" and "&nGt;" stay as written
h-value-nbsp-stays    strings.TrimSpace trims U+00A0, U+0085 and 23 more code points from a header value
h-name-ascii-case-only  strings.ToLower reads "Content-D" U+0130 "sposition" as Content-Disposition
c-label-not-ascii     htmlindex.Get lowercases a label by Unicode: U+212A "oi8-r" names koi8-r
c-replacement-empty   a part labelled iso-2022-kr or hz-gb-2312 decodes to one U+FFFD, even when it is empty
p-section-signed      strconv.Atoi reads "filename*+0" as section 0, and a section number past 2^31 parses on
                      64-bit legs and fails on 32-bit ones
w-b-carriage-return   base64 inside an encoded word skips a CR
```

§11.14's determinism row forbids "library-version input", and QD-474 keeps the HTML parser out for that reason. The same holds for these calls: a Go release that fixes the 4,096 B limit, or the 32-bit sum, changes which bytes a writer indexes, and then every reader built on the other release reports an honest writer. The Unicode version is pinned and checked at start; the standard library's parsers are not, and cannot be, since they carry no version of their own.

*C. Nothing bounds memory.* Both extractors hold the message, each part decoded, each part again in UTF-8 and the joined text at once: the landed one allocates 2.5 times a 50 MiB message that is one base64 text part, and 8 to 10 times a small HTML message (11.4). §11.15 gives the iOS app 4 MiB of working set and "never a whole file ... over 1 MiB in RAM", and the owner directed on 2026-11-10 that bulk state lives in storage (QD-641). A one-pass reading in fixed memory is not possible under the rules as the two read them, because three of them need unbounded lookahead: a header value of any length is joined before its encoded words decode; a delimiter line may carry any run of trailing whitespace; so may a quoted-printable soft line break.

*D. Field order and placement are unstated* (question search-m10-07-extractor-field-placement): where a file's path goes, where attachment names go among the text parts, how To and Cc and several parts join, and what each chunk past the first carries. The two implementations took the same readings, pending an answer.

**Sizes.** D-EVS-59 makes every `SearchRequest` body exactly 4,016 B and every `SearchReply` body exactly steps × 16,384 B, so that a relay learns nothing from a length. The only filler is `pad`, proto field 15: one tag byte, a varint length, then zeros, and proto3 leaves an empty field out. So `pad` adds 0 bytes, or 3 to 129 (a one-byte length), or 131 to 16,386 (two), or 16,388 and more (three). It cannot add 1, 2, 130 or 16,387. Run against the marshaler for every pad length to 70,000, those four are the only gaps up to 65,536. Concretely:

```text
a request whose other fields encode to 4,015 B, 4,014 B or 3,886 B       cannot be made 4,016 B
a one-step reply whose other fields encode to 16,383, 16,382 or 16,254 B cannot be made 16,384 B
a two-step reply whose other fields encode to 16,381 B                   cannot be made 32,768 B
   (three steps: 32,765 B; four: 49,149 B)
```

A reply reaches these whenever its hits nearly fill a step: the size tests of 11.3 build replies of 6, 11 and 17 hits that sit exactly on the last gap at two, three and four steps. The owner decided the approach on 2026-11-06 (QD-215): no wire change, every other field stops 131 B short of the body's size, a multi-step reply "holds one hit back", and `SearchFilters` is capped at 768 B. What that leaves open is everything an implementer needs:

- the pad's length as a function, and which contents are refused;
- which hits a reply keeps, when the fields that describe the page (`complete`, `checked_through_ms`, `counts`) change size with the hits kept;
- a proof that a request always fits and that a reply with a hit to give always returns one, which needs a cap on every field, and two fields have none (`SearchHit.correction`, `SearchCoverage.chain`);
- what a receiver checks. "A non-zero pad" is INVALID (§11.14's status row), but a body can carry `pad` twice, the parser keeping the last, or carry a field this version does not know, and either hides non-zero bytes from that check;
- the landed `padSearchReply` (`rpc_search.go`), which tries five pad lengths and fails on a gap, after which its caller answers a small `UNAVAILABLE` Error: a failure after parsing that is not padded, which D-EVS-59 forbids.

### 11.2 The design

Extraction is one function, written out below in full. It calls no parser of the standard library or of any module: base64, quoted-printable, character references, header fields, parameters and multipart bodies are each a rule here. What it takes from outside is tables, each pinned: Unicode 17.0.0 and the charset decoders, both from golang.org/x/text v0.43.0 and Go's `unicode` package, which normalizer 1 already pins and checks at start; HTML's named character references, a list its standard has frozen, held in `entities.json`; and the block tags, listed here. Three limits, HeaderMax, LineWindow and MimeDepth, make it computable in one pass with fixed memory (11.2.8). It is total: every byte string has exactly one output and there is no error to return.

The identifiers stay extractor 1 and normalizer 1. Index format 1 freezes at M10's exit (§23.8) and no index exists outside tests, so this section defines extractor 1 rather than adding a second. `protocol/INDEX-FORMAT.md`'s Extractor 1 and Documents sections are replaced by 11.8's text.

Bodies keep the owner's rule, made exact: one function gives the pad's length, one predicate says which contents can be sized, the builders keep contents inside it by caps that 11.3 proves sufficient, and a receiver accepts a body only if it is the one encoding of its message. `search.proto` does not change.

#### 11.2.1 Terms, constants and tables

```text
LF 0x0A   CR 0x0D   SP 0x20   HT 0x09
white      the bytes 0x09 to 0x0D and 0x20
blank      SP and HT
well-formed UTF-8   Unicode's table 3-7 (RFC 3629): no overlong form, no surrogate, nothing past U+10FFFF
lower(x)   x with each byte 0x41-0x5A raised by 0x20, every other byte as it is; "ignoring case" means equal
           under lower
trim(x)    x without its leading and its trailing white bytes
letter     A-Z and a-z; digit 0-9; alphanumeric either; hex digit 0-9, A-F and a-f
```

No rule below reads a header, a parameter, a label, a tag name or an encoding's name as Unicode text: names compare under `lower`, and only white bytes are trimmed. Constants are facts of the format, never settings:

```text
HeaderMax       16,384 B   a logical header line, and the joined values of one field name (H4, H6)
LineWindow       1,024 B   the longest delimiter line (B1); the longest blank run inside a soft line break (T3)
MimeDepth           16     the multipart levels entered (M2)
ChunkBytes   1,048,576 B   a document's share of its source's text (D4)
Overlap            256 B   what a document repeats of the next (D4)
SniffWindow      8,000 B   the bytes that decide text or binary (S2)
TitleMax            80 B   a file's title (S4)
FieldCut         1,024 B   normalized subject, from, to and title (N6)
KeySetMax      524,288 B   a key set's encoding, past which its document is skipped (D6)
ShardLone          128 B   what D6 counts for the header, doc_key, version and time of a shard holding one
                           document; D6 reads ShardBody, 1,032,192 B, from 1.2.1 (amended 2026-11-12, QD-760)
```

Tables, each part of extractor 1 or normalizer 1:

```text
Unicode       17.0.0: general categories and scripts from Go's unicode package (unicode.Version), normalization
              and case folding from golang.org/x/text v0.43.0 (norm.Version, cases.UnicodeVersion). A build
              linking anything else is another normalizer and writes nothing (INDEX-FORMAT.md's Tables).
charsets      golang.org/x/text v0.43.0's encoding/htmlindex: 228 labels naming 40 encodings, listed in
              charsets.json (SHA-256 9c94ee72a1db3f894cd3765b3805839835b66fcca57f9530cbee31968b36a4da), and
              that module's decoder for each (C1-C3)
references    HTML's 2,231 named character references, 106 of them also without their ';' and 93 of them two
              code points: entities.json, SHA-256 9e7bac4a454044f307050b23fefa224beea56525742cc4774e1d4c6da6d40e57
block tags    address article aside blockquote br center dd details dialog dir div dl dt fieldset figcaption
              figure footer form h1 h2 h3 h4 h5 h6 header hgroup hr li main menu nav ol p pre section summary
              table tbody td tfoot th thead tr ul                                              (44 names; X4)
C1 table      what numeric references 128 to 159 mean, in order (E1): U+20AC 0081 201A 0192 201E 2026 2020 2021
              02C6 2030 0160 2039 0152 008D 017D 008F 0090 2018 2019 201C 201D 2022 2013 2014 02DC 2122 0161
              203A 0153 009D 017E 0178
```

#### 11.2.2 Normalizer 1, whole

Normalizer 1 is `protocol/INDEX-FORMAT.md`'s, unchanged. It is restated here with every byte §11.14's text row leaves open, so that this section holds the whole path from a file's bytes to a key set.

```text
N1  Each byte that does not begin a well-formed UTF-8 sequence becomes U+FFFD, one for each such byte: an
    overlong form, a surrogate, a value past U+10FFFF and a sequence cut short by the end of the value each
    give one U+FFFD a byte. A well-formed U+FFFD stays.
N2  NFKC, as x/text's norm.NFKC gives it, its stream-safe rule included: after 30 non-starters it inserts
    U+034F.
N3  Full case folding, as x/text's cases.Fold() gives it with no locale, then U+AB70-U+ABBF to
    U+13A0-U+13EF and U+13F8-U+13FD to U+13F0-U+13F5 (QD-256).
N4  NFD. Then each code point of category Mn is dropped when the nearest code point before it in the value
    that is not Mn is of category L and of script Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic or Hebrew (the Script
    property, not Script_Extensions). With no such code point before it, at a value's start, it stays. Then
    NFC.
N5  Each maximal run of code points outside categories L, M and N becomes one SP. U+FFFD is in such a run.
N6  For fields 1 to 4, the result is cut to its longest prefix of at most FieldCut bytes that ends on a code
    point.
N7  A document's text is, for each field in number order whose normalized value is not empty: SP, that
    value, SP. Nothing is trimmed, so a value that normalizes to a leading or trailing space shows two.
N8  A document's key set is the distinct values b0 x 65,536 + b1 x 256 + b2 over every three consecutive
    bytes of its text, the windows across two fields' padding included. A text under 3 B has none.
```

What the row left open, and how each is settled: N1 counts bytes, not maximal subparts. N1 to N5 run on each field's value by itself, with N4's "nearest code point before" starting afresh, and on each chunk by itself, so a chunk that begins or ends inside a character shows U+FFFD there. N6 cuts after N5, on normalized bytes, and may cut between a base and a mark N4 kept. No step maps a code point to nothing but N4, which keeps the letter, so a value that is not empty never normalizes to nothing, and N7's test reads the same on the value before normalization.

#### 11.2.3 Documents: kinds, fields, chunks and rows

```text
D1  A version is extracted as mail when its repo is a mailbox, or a general repo laid out as a group inbox
    (§15.7), and its path begins "m/". Every other version that §11.14's never row lets in is extracted as a
    file. A record entry's or a derived document's fields are its class's (§16.8, §16.11).
D2  A file that S1-S3 find to be text has, for each chunk c of its text (D4), one document: field 4 is the
    file's title (S4), one SP and the path's bytes; field 5 is c. Field 4 has that form even when the title
    is empty. Fields 1-3 are empty.
D3  A message has, for each chunk c of its body text, one document: field 1 is the decoded Subject, field 2
    the decoded From, field 3 the decoded To and the decoded Cc, each left out when empty and joined by one
    SP when both stand, and field 5 is c. Field 4 is empty. "Decoded X" is W applied to H6's joined value of
    X, of the message's own header block alone. The body text is the walk's pieces (M1-M6) in the order the
    walk gives them, the empty ones left out, joined by one SP.
D4  The chunks of a text t are t[k x ChunkBytes : min(len(t), (k+1) x ChunkBytes + Overlap)] for k = 0, 1, ...
    while k x ChunkBytes < len(t), and the one empty chunk when t is empty. Chunk k is the document with
    chunk number k. Bytes are counted in the text as extracted (a file's after S1 and S3, a message's body
    text), before normalization. Every chunk carries the same fields 1-4.
D5  A document's row is INDEX-FORMAT.md's: its locator the path's bytes, its subject, from and to the values
    of fields 1-3 before normalization, its title the title of S4 alone, never the path, each with N1 applied
    and then cut by that file's Trimming; its size the length in bytes of the whole file or message, the
    same on every chunk's row.
D6  (amended 2026-11-12, QD-760) A document d is skipped when its key set would encode past KeySetMax, or
    when d alone would not fit a shard: lone(d) > ShardBody, with
        lone(d) = ShardLone + len(row) + dict(K) + n
        row     d's row as its entry carries it (D5; ref_id included in ur/index), at most 2,048 B
        K       d's key set, k_1 < ... < k_n; n counts the postings, one byte a key
        dict(K) = vlen(B) + the sum over blocks j = 0 .. B - 1 of (3 + vlen(o_j) + vlen(64 x j))
                  + the sum over i = 1 .. n of (6 - p_i), with B = ceil(n / 64); 1 when n = 0
        p_i     0 when k_i is the first key of its block (i mod 64 = 1); else 2 when k_i and k_(i-1) have
                the same two high bytes, 1 when only the same high byte, else 0
        o_j     the sum of (6 - p_i) over the keys before block j, i <= 64 x j
        vlen(x) the length of x as a VByte
    A skipped document has no entry, and where its key was indexed before, its version is a tombstone
    (§11.14's sniff row). The test reads the key set and the row and nothing else, so the device that
    extracts, a reproducer and a decoder compute it alike.
```

**What lone(d) is** (amended 2026-11-12, QD-760; question search-m10-10-document-past-a-shard, option 1). It is the encoded length, before its pad, of a shard that holds d alone (INDEX-FORMAT.md's Shards), with one part made a constant. The doc table's row, the dictionary in blocks of 64 and the postings are counted byte for byte: a key's entry is its flag byte, the 3 - p bytes its block's previous key does not share, and one byte each for a document count of 1 and a list length of 1; a block's index row is its first key, its entries offset o_j and its list offset 64 x j; each list is the one byte 0x01. The rest, which is the magic, the header and its length, the doc_key, the version and the time, moves with the bucket's day, the pad generation and the version, none of which the extracting device and a later merger share, so D6 counts it as ShardLone. In format 1 it is at most 95 B: 4 for the magic, 1 for the header's length, a header of at most 54 B with every number at its widest, 16 for the doc_key and 10 each for the version and the time. So a shard holding a kept document alone encodes at least 33 B under ShardBody, in a bucket and in all, whoever writes it and when, which is what 1.2.4's `take` needs of a new shard.

Measured against the landed encoder (`indexShardBuilder.encodeUnpadded`) on 2026-11-12: dict(K) + n equals the encoder's dictionary and postings on 32 key sets (none, 1, 63, 64 and 65 keys, dense runs up to 150,000, steps of 256, 257, 3,000 and 65,536, and twenty random sets of up to 60,000 keys); the constant part is 60 B in an all shard, 66 B in a bucket shard as the tests build one and 95 B at the widest; and keys 0 to n - 1 under a 36 B row give lone = 1,032,192 at n = 199,608, kept, whose shard at the widest header is 1,032,159 B, and 1,032,197 at n = 199,609, skipped.

What it skips. A key costs at least 5 B in a shard of its own, a 4 B entry and a 1 B list, and at least 1 B in a key set. A key set past KeySetMax has more than 392,000 keys (each gap takes one byte, and the gaps' further bytes number at most 132,104, since the gaps sum to at most 2^24), so it fails the shard test too: KeySetMax stays as the entry codec's cap and as the test that needs no pass over the keys. A document of up to 144,000 keys always passes (7 B a key and 9 B a block at most, under a 2,048 B row), and none of more than 206,438 does; between the two the prefixes its keys share decide. Under normalizer 1 few texts get there. A 1 MiB chunk of base64, the question's example, folds to 37 symbols (N3, N5) and has 50,572 keys, lone 262,774; random code points of the BMP, as noise read as UTF-16 gives, 196,095 keys and lone 1,025,349, kept. What passes the bound is a chunk of letters from many scripts with little repeated: letters drawn at random from the BMP's 1,380 two-byte and 47,549 three-byte letters give 327,272 keys in 1 MiB, a key set of 333,861 B and lone 1,703,722, and with ASCII letters and digits among them 470,197 keys in a key set of 475,931 B, still within KeySetMax. Such a document was kept before this amendment and no shard could hold it; it is now skipped, and is not searchable, as a document past KeySetMax already was not.

D2, D3 and D4 are question search-m10-07-extractor-field-placement's option 1. A path's words are found through field 4. A message's attachment names sit in field 5 where their parts stand, so a phrase can span a name and the text beside it only as they are laid out in the message. Field 4's cut (N6) means a path's tail past 1,024 normalized bytes of title and path is not indexed.

A document's `doc_key`, version and attributes are not extraction's: `doc_key` is INDEX-FORMAT.md's Documents, from the path's bytes and the chunk number. The path given to extraction is the path's own bytes, the same in every path epoch: a cut-over (section 9) gives an index ref's files new tokens like any other path's, and changes no document, row or key. Nor does anything here change a stored size: slots, large entries and shards keep §11.14's sizes and pads, under section 2's rules for staged and versionless content, and 11.2.9's sizes are of messages between two devices, which evs never holds.

#### 11.2.4 Files

```text
S1  A file that begins FE FF is UTF-16 big-endian, and one that begins FF FE little-endian. The mark is
    dropped. Each two bytes after it are a code unit; a surrogate pair is its code point; a surrogate with no
    partner is U+FFFD; an odd last byte is U+FFFD. The text is the result in UTF-8, and the file is text.
    Nothing else is asked of it: U+0000 is allowed.
S2  Otherwise take the window, the file's first SniffWindow bytes or the whole file when it is shorter. The
    file is binary, and gives no document, when the window holds a byte 0x00, or when, reading well-formed
    UTF-8 sequences from the window's start, a byte is met that does not begin one, unless the bytes from
    there to the window's end are a proper prefix of a well-formed sequence (a character the window cut).
    The prefix test is exact: E0 80, ED A0 and F4 90 begin nothing. Otherwise the file is text, and its text
    is all of its bytes, whatever lies past the window.
S3  A text of S2 that begins EF BB BF loses those three bytes, once.
S4  The title: split the text at each LF. The title line is the first line that holds a code point of
    category L or N, reading the line as UTF-8 with N1's rule (so U+FFFD, which is neither, stands for each
    ill-formed byte). Take that line; drop its leading run of '#' and SP bytes; drop its trailing run of SP,
    HT and CR bytes; apply N1; cut to the longest prefix of at most TitleMax bytes that ends on a code point.
    No such line: the title is empty.
```

S3 is new: without it a file saved with a UTF-8 mark shows the mark and its heading's "# " in its title.

#### 11.2.5 Mail

A message is read as RFC 5322 and MIME lay it out, by the rules below and no others. `extract_mail(content)`:

```text
fields, body = header_block(content)                                      H1-H5
subject = words(joined(fields, "subject"))                                H6, W
from    = words(joined(fields, "from"))
to      = join_nonempty(words(joined(fields, "to")), words(joined(fields, "cc")))
pieces  = []
walk(fields, body, 0, pieces)                                             M1-M6
text    = join_nonempty(pieces...)             the non-empty ones, in order, with one SP between
one document per chunk of text (D3, D4)
```

**The header block.**

```text
H1  Lines end at LF. A line's content is its bytes before the LF, less one CR when it ends in one. The last
    line may end at the end of the input instead.
H2  The header block is the lines from the start up to the first line whose content is empty. That line
    belongs to neither part; the body is everything after its LF. With no empty line, everything is header
    and the body is empty. A line of only blank bytes is not empty.
H3  A line whose first byte is blank, when a logical line stands before it, is appended to that logical
    line as it is, its leading blank bytes included. Any other line begins a logical line.
H4  A logical line is at most HeaderMax bytes: bytes past that are dropped as they arrive.
H5  A logical line with no ':' is no field. Otherwise its name is lower(trim(bytes before the first ':'))
    and its value is trim(bytes after it). Fields keep their order.
H6  first(name) is the value of the first field of that name, or empty. joined(name) is the values of every
    field of that name, in order, with one SP between each two, an empty value included, cut to its first
    HeaderMax bytes.
```

**Encoded words** (RFC 2047). `words(v)` scans v from the left:

```text
W1  An encoded word is "=?" C "?" E "?" T "?=", where C, E and T hold no '?', and E is one byte: B, b, Q
    or q. It may stand anywhere in v, inside a token too.
W2  Its charset is C up to its first '*'. It is not an encoded word when the charset is empty, when the
    charset or T holds a blank byte, or when W3 or W4 refuses T. Its text is T decoded by W3 or W4 and then
    as the charset's label says (C1-C3).
W3  B: drop every '=' at T's end. What is left must be base64 alphabet bytes (A-Z a-z 0-9 + /) and not 1
    more than a multiple of 4 long, or T is refused. Each 4 bytes give 3; a last 2 give 1 and a last 3 give
    2, the unused bits ignored. An empty T decodes to nothing.
W4  Q: '_' is SP; '=' and two hex digits are that byte; '=' followed by anything else, or by fewer than two
    bytes, refuses T; every other byte is itself.
W5  Find the leftmost "=?" at or after the scan position. If an encoded word starts there, take it and move
    the position past its "?="; if not, move the position 2 bytes on and look again. When none is left, the
    rest of v is text.
W6  The text between two encoded words is dropped when it is empty or only blank bytes, and kept otherwise.
    Text before the first word and after the last is kept. So is text between a word and something that is
    not one.
```

**Media values and parameters** (RFC 2045, 2183, 2231), for Content-Type and Content-Disposition:

```text
P1  The value is lower(trim(bytes before the first ';')). An absent or empty field has the empty value and
    no parameters.
P2  The bytes after the first ';' are split at each ';' that is outside quotes. A '"' opens quotes and the
    next '"' closes them; inside quotes a '\' and the byte after it are passed over together. A quote left
    open runs to the end.
P3  A piece with no '=' is no parameter. Otherwise its name is lower(trim(bytes before the first '=')) and
    its raw value trim(bytes after it). A name ending in '*' is extended, and loses that '*'. If the name
    then holds a '*', the bytes before the first one are the parameter's name and the bytes after it its
    section, which must be 1 to 9 digits and nothing else, or the piece is no parameter. So a parameter has
    up to three kinds of piece: plain, extended, and sections 0, 1, ..., each plain or extended. Of two
    pieces of one name and kind (and one section number), the first counts.
P4  A plain piece's value is its raw value unquoted: when it is at least 2 bytes and begins and ends with
    '"', those two go, and inside, a '\' followed by a byte gives that byte. Anything else is as written. An
    extended piece's raw value is never unquoted.
P5  param(name), in this order: (a) if it has a section 0, join sections 0, 1, 2, ... up to the first
    number that is missing; if the result is not empty, that is the value; (b) else its extended piece;
    (c) else its plain piece; (d) else empty.
P6  An extended value is charset ' language ' text when it holds two "'" (the first two split it), and
    otherwise all text with no charset. Its text is percent-decoded: '%' and two hex digits are that byte;
    if any '%' is followed by anything else, the whole text stands as written. In (a), an extended section
    is percent-decoded, a plain one is not, and only section 0, when extended, is split for a charset. The
    bytes are then decoded as that charset's label says (C1-C3).
```

**Charsets.**

```text
C1  A label is trimmed. It names an encoding when every byte of it is 0x21 to 0x7E and lower(label) is one
    of charsets.json's 228 labels.
C2  No label, a label that names nothing, and a label that names utf-8 or replacement leave the bytes as
    they are. Ill-formed UTF-8 then meets N1.
C3  Any other label's bytes are decoded by x/text v0.43.0's decoder for its encoding. Those decoders answer
    malformed input with U+FFFD and never fail. No charset is guessed from content.
```

**The walk.** `walk(fields, body, depth, pieces)`:

```text
M1  type = P(first("content-type")), disposition = P(first("content-disposition")). The media type is
    type's value. When that is empty it is text/plain, or message/rfc822 for a part directly inside a
    multipart/digest (RFC 2046); type's parameters stand either way.
M2  A media type beginning "multipart/": let b = type.param("boundary"). If b is empty, or depth >=
    MimeDepth, the entity gives nothing. Otherwise for each part of parts(body, b) (B1-B4), in order:
    walk(header_block(part), depth + 1). The entity's own name is not read. Every part is walked, the parts
    of multipart/alternative like any others.
M3  Any other entity: its name is disposition.param("filename"), or when that is empty type.param("name").
    A name that is not empty gives the piece words(name).
M4  If disposition's value is "attachment", the entity gives nothing more.
M5  text/plain gives the piece: transfer(first("content-transfer-encoding"), body), decoded as the label
    type.param("charset") says (C1-C3). text/html gives html_to_text of the same (11.2.6).
M6  Every other media type gives nothing more: no bytes of it are decoded, and a message/rfc822 part is not
    entered.
```

**Multipart bodies.** `parts(body, b)`:

```text
B1  Split body into lines at each LF (a line's bytes exclude the LF; the last line may end at the end). A
    line is a delimiter line when it is at most LineWindow bytes and, without its trailing run of SP, HT and
    CR bytes, equals "--" b; it is the close delimiter when it equals "--" b "--". The comparison is of
    bytes, from the line's first byte.
B2  A part begins after a delimiter line's LF and ends before the next delimiter or close delimiter line,
    less that line's own break: when the part's last byte is LF it goes, and then a CR before it goes.
B3  Lines before the first delimiter line belong to no part. At the close delimiter the parts end, and
    whatever follows it belongs to none.
B4  With no close delimiter, the last part runs to the end of body and keeps its last line break.
```

When a line is a delimiter of two nested multiparts, the outer one takes it, since the inner body is cut out of an outer part before it is split. A boundary that ends in SP, HT or CR, or is longer than 1,022 B, matches no line, and its multipart gives nothing.

**Transfer encodings.** `transfer(e, body)`:

```text
T1  lower(trim(e)) equal to "base64" selects T2 and "quoted-printable" T3. Anything else, absent included,
    leaves body as it is.
T2  base64: white bytes are skipped. Alphabet bytes are taken up to the first byte that is neither, '='
    included, where decoding ends. Each 4 give 3 bytes; at the end a last 2 give 1 and a last 3 give 2, the
    unused bits ignored; a last 1 gives none.
T3  quoted-printable, left to right: '=' and two hex digits are that byte. Any other '=' is a soft line
    break, which gives nothing, when after it come at most LineWindow blank bytes and then LF, or CR LF, or
    the end of body; all of that is consumed. Any other '=' is itself. Every other byte is itself, control
    bytes included. No line is too long, and trailing blank bytes of a line stay.
```

#### 11.2.6 HTML to text

`html_to_text(t)` is `references(tags(t))`: every tag goes first, and character references are decoded in what is left, once. Whitespace is copied as it stands, line breaks included, and N5 folds it. Nothing is read from an attribute: no `alt`, `title` or `href` reaches the text. An element's text is kept whatever the element, `script` and `style` apart: `title`, `option`, `noscript` and `textarea` give their text, and since `title`, `head`, `body`, `caption` and `option` are not block tags, a document's title joins its first body word (vector `x-document`).

**Tags.** `tags(t)` reads t from the left. A byte other than '<' is copied. At a '<':

```text
X1  "<!--" opens a comment, which ends after the first "-->" that begins 4 or more bytes past the '<'. It
    gives nothing.
X2  Otherwise "<!" or "<?" opens a declaration, which ends after the next '>'. It gives nothing.
X3  Otherwise '<' followed by a letter or '/' opens a tag, which ends at the first '>' outside quotes,
    looking from the byte after the '<': a '"' or a "'" opens quotes and the next byte equal to it closes
    them. The tag is a closing tag when the byte after '<' is '/'.
X4  The tag's name is lower of the alphanumeric bytes that follow the '<', or the "</", up to the first
    byte that is not one, and may be empty. A tag whose name is a block tag gives one SP, closing or not.
    Any other tag gives nothing.
X5  A tag named script or style that is not a closing tag also takes its content: look, from the byte
    after the tag's '>', for the first "</" followed by that name ignoring case and then by the end of t or
    a byte that is not alphanumeric. That "</" opens a tag by X3, and reading resumes after its '>'. All of
    it gives nothing, the SP of X4 too, since neither name is a block tag.
X6  Any other '<' is copied.
X7  A comment, declaration or tag with no end, a script or style with no end tag, and an end tag with no
    '>' each take everything to the end of t.
```

**Character references.** `references(u)` reads u from the left. A byte other than '&' is copied. At an '&':

```text
E1  "&#", then an optional 'x' or 'X', then one or more digits (hex digits after an x), then an optional
    ';' is a numeric reference; all of it is consumed. Its value is the digits' number, held at 0x110000
    once it passes that. A value 0x80 to 0x9F gives the C1 table's code point; 0, 0xD800 to 0xDFFF and
    anything past 0x10FFFF give U+FFFD; any other value gives that code point. With no digit, the '&' is
    copied and reading goes on after it.
E2  Otherwise take the alphanumeric bytes after the '&', as many as there are. With none, the '&' is copied
    and reading goes on after it. Else the name is those bytes and a ';' if one follows them. If the name is
    one of the 2,231, its one or two code points are given and all of it is consumed. Names match by exact
    bytes: "AMP;" is one and "Amp;" is not.
E3  Otherwise, for k = min(6, the name's length - 1) down to 2: if the name's first k bytes are one of the
    106 names without ';', its code point is given and the '&' and those k bytes are consumed. The first k
    that matches counts.
E4  Otherwise the '&' and the name are copied.
```

E1 to E4 are HTML's own rule for text outside attributes, with its table whole. They are not `html.UnescapeString`: 11.1 B lists the four places that function departs from them.

#### 11.2.7 Malformed input

Nothing is refused and nothing is guessed. Each kind of damage has one reading, already given by a rule; this table collects them.

```text
no empty line after the header                 all header, empty body (H2)
a header line with no ':'                      passed over; a continuation still joins it (H3, H5)
a field or a joined value past 16,384 B        its first 16,384 B (H4, H6)
several Subject, From, To or Cc fields         all, joined by SP before their words decode (H6)
several Content-Type fields                    the first (H6)
an encoded word that breaks W1-W4              text, as written
an unknown charset, or none                    the bytes as they are; N1 maps what is not UTF-8 (C2)
a multipart with no boundary, or 17 deep       nothing from it (M2)
a part with no header, or no blank line        text/plain, or all header and an empty body (M1, H2)
a digest's part with no Content-Type           message/rfc822: not entered (M1, M6)
no close delimiter                             the last part runs to the end (B4)
a delimiter line past 1,024 B                  not a delimiter: it is part of the body (B1)
base64 with a byte outside its alphabet        what came before it, the last partial group decoded (T2)
an '=' that is neither an escape nor a break   itself (T3)
an unknown transfer encoding                   the body as it is (T1)
a tag, comment or script with no end           everything after it is dropped (X7)
a reference that names nothing                 text, as written (E4)
a file with a NUL or ill-formed UTF-8 in       binary: no document; where it was indexed, a tombstone (S2;
  its first 8,000 B                              §11.14's sniff row)
ill-formed UTF-8 past 8,000 B                  U+FFFD a byte, at normalization (N1)
a chunk whose key set passes 512 KiB           skipped (D6)
a chunk that alone would not fit a shard       skipped (D6's lone(d); amended 2026-11-12, QD-760)
```

#### 11.2.8 One pass, fixed memory

The rules above are written over whole values. Each was chosen so that the same function can be computed in one pass over the message with a fixed amount of memory, and SEARCH-M10-44 builds that form for app hosts. A stage reads the bytes the stage before it gives:

```text
stage                    what it keeps                                         from
lines and delimiters     the current line's first 1,024 B; one held line       B1, B2
                         break; up to 16 boundaries of at most 1,022 B
header blocks            the logical line being read, 16,384 B; per entity,    H4, H6
                         the first Content-Type, -Disposition and -Transfer-
                         Encoding values; for the message, the four joined
                         values; 16,384 B each
base64                   up to 3 alphabet bytes                                T2
quoted-printable         an '=' and up to 1,024 blank bytes and a CR           T3
charset                  the decoder's state, a few bytes                      C3
tags                     a state, a quote byte, 8 B of a name, up to 8 B of    X1-X7
                         a match in progress
references               an '&' and up to 33 B                                 E1-E3
pieces                   whether anything was given yet                        D3
chunks                   the 256 B that two documents share                    D4
normalizer and key set   INDEX-FORMAT.md's: a few KiB, and the key bitmap      N1-N8
```

Four points are not obvious. (1) A line is tested as a delimiter against every open boundary, outermost first, once its LF arrives or 1,024 B have passed without one; a line break is held back until the next line is known not to be a delimiter, and dropped when it is one (B2). (2) A header line of interest is kept to 16,384 B and the rest of it discarded as it arrives; every other header line is discarded whole. (3) A document's key set is collected while its text passes; at a chunk's end the next 256 B are fed to it, the document is finished, and the same 256 B begin the next, so one key bitmap is live at a time. (4) A file's title is needed by its first document, and may lie anywhere in the file: the file is in storage, so the title is found by a first read that stops at the first line with a letter or a number, which for nearly every file is its first line, and the documents are built by a second.

A reference's 33 B is enough: the longest name is 32 B with its ';', so a run of more than 31 alphanumeric bytes matches no name whole, E3 looks at its first 6 bytes, and whatever E4 copies needs no second look, since no alphanumeric byte opens a reference. A numeric reference keeps its number, held at 0x110000, and no digits. A tag's 8 B of name is enough: the longest name that matters is 10 B (blockquote, figcaption), and a longer run is compared as it arrives against the 44 names without being kept.

#### 11.2.9 Exact body sizes

A body is the deterministic proto3 encoding of its message, in which `pad`, the highest-numbered field of both messages, comes last. Write *content* for the length in bytes of that encoding with `pad` empty, and *size* for what the body must be: 4,016 for a request, steps × 16,384 for a reply, steps being the request's (1 to 4).

```text
Z1  A pad of L > 0 zero bytes encodes as 0x7A, L as a varint, and the L bytes: L + 2 bytes for L up to
    127, L + 3 up to 16,383, L + 4 up to 2,097,151.
Z2  pad_length(size, content): let gap = size - content. If 131 <= gap <= 16,386, L = gap - 3. If 16,388
    <= gap <= 2,097,155, L = gap - 4. Otherwise there is none.
Z3  A content is admissible for a size when 0 <= content <= size - 131 and size - content is not 16,387.
    Builders build only admissible contents, and for those Z2 always answers.
Z4  Caps, which builders keep and receivers check:
      SearchRequest   query at most 512 B (its 16 terms are the grammar's to count, §16.10); at most 64
                      repos; a repo_id 16 B and a ref_id 16 B or empty; filters at most 768 B as encoded
                      (QD-215); steps 1 to 4
      SearchReply     at most 64 coverage rows, each with 16 B ids and a chain of at most 32 B; at most 20
                      hits
      SearchHit       ids and signer 16 B; locator at most 512 B; correction at most 256 B; at most 8
                      fields, each text at most 256 B; snippet at most 200 B
Z5  A request is built by filling its fields within Z4, a page above 0 carrying none of page 0's (§11.14's
    exchange row), taking its content, and setting pad to pad_length(4,016, content) zero bytes. Within Z4
    a request's content is at most 3,778 B on page 0 and 36 B on a later page, so it is always admissible.
    A search that would break a cap is not sent: one whose filters pass 768 B stays on the device
    (QD-215), and more than 64 repos go in further requests (§11.14's order row).
Z6  A reply is built from the hits still to give, in rank order and each within Z4, and a function head(k)
    that gives the reply's other fields when the first k of them are returned (status, phase, complete,
    checked_through_ms, counts, and on page 0 the coverage rows). For k from min(20, the number to give)
    down to 0: take the content of head(k) with those k hits; the first k whose content is admissible is
    the reply, padded by Z2. Hits past k stay with the cursor for the next page. k = 0 is always
    admissible, and so is k = 1 when there is a hit (11.3), so a page with a hit to give returns at least
    one.
Z7  A failure after parsing is a reply of its status alone, with the version fields and, where the request
    parsed, its search_id and page. Its content is at most 90 B, so it is admissible at every size.
Z8  A receiver accepts a body only when all of these hold, checked in this order:
      (a) its length is the size: 4,016 B for a request; for a reply, the steps the requester asked times
          16,384;
      (b) it parses as its message;
      (c) for a request, its search_version is one this build supports;
      (d) it is the one encoding of its message (Z9): it holds no field this build does not know, at any
          depth, and marshaling the parsed message deterministically gives the same bytes;
      (e) every byte of pad is zero;
      (f) its fields are within Z4.
    An indexer answers a request that fails (a), (b), (d), (e) or (f) with status INVALID and one that
    fails (c) with UNSUPPORTED_VERSION, each by Z7 at the request's steps where (b) held and steps is 1 to
    4, and at one step otherwise. A requester treats a reply that fails (a) to (e), or that names another
    search_id or page than it asked, as no reply: the indexer failed, and §11.14's failover row applies. For
    (f) on a reply it drops what is past a cap and keeps the rest: coverage rows past 64 and one with a
    wrong-length id or a chain past 32 B; hits past 20 and one with a wrong-length id or a locator past
    512 B; a hit's fields past 8; and a field, snippet or correction past its length.
Z9  The one encoding of a message is what proto.MarshalOptions{Deterministic: true} writes for it, these
    messages holding no map. As a rule of bytes: its fields stand in ascending number, a field once unless it
    is repeated, a repeated field's elements together and in order; a number or bool that is zero and a
    string or bytes that is empty are left out, unless they are an element of a repeated field; a message
    field is written when it is present, though it be empty; every varint is at its shortest;
    SearchFilters.kinds is one packed record, left out when it has no element; and a message field's bytes
    are that message's one encoding.
```

Z8 (d) is what makes (e) mean anything. By Z9 a body that passes (d) has exactly one `pad`, at its end, and nothing in it that the parser did not read. Both halves of (d) are needed: the marshaler writes back a field it does not know, so a body carrying one after `pad` marshals to itself. (c) comes before (d) so that a request of a later version, which may carry fields this build does not know, is told UNSUPPORTED_VERSION and not INVALID. What a requester makes of a reply's version, status and served codes is SEARCH-M10-31's as planned: an unknown one is never read as OK or served.

**Why the rule is a builder's and not the wire's.** No field can add one byte: the shortest is a tag and a one-byte value. So whatever fields a body had, a content one byte short of its size could not be filled, and some rule must keep builders away from it. Given such a rule, stopping 131 B short costs 0.8% of a step and leaves one gap, 16,387, which only a reply of two or more steps can meet and Z6 steps around. A second filler field would close that gap and give a receiver a second thing to check; proto3 has no fixed-width length; a varint longer than it need be is what §22.6 forbids. This is QD-215's choice, and 11.3 shows it is enough.

**Wire changes.** None to `search.proto`'s fields or numbers. Three comments change (11.8): `SearchHit.correction` gains "<= 256 B", `SearchCoverage.chain` "<= 32 B", and `SearchFilters` "<= 768 B encoded". §11.14's status row gains Z8 (d)'s refusal.

**What others build on.** Problem 1 (merges, roll-ups and the journal) may rely on: an entry is a function of its own document; a document is a function of its path's bytes, its version's bytes and the tables of 11.2.1; a version's documents are numbered 0 to n - 1 with n = max(1, ⌈len(text) / ChunkBytes⌉), so a version with fewer chunks than the one before leaves tombstones for exactly the chunk numbers from its n up; two builds that extract one version write equal rows and key sets, so a merge never needs the text, and a host with the text checks an entry by building it. Problem 7 (remote search) may rely on Z2, Z3 and Z6 as functions, on Z7 for every failure after parsing, and on Z8's order; it owns what `head(k)` computes.
