### 11.3 Invariants and why they hold

No part of this is concurrent: extraction and sizing are pure functions, so there is no model. The proofs are arguments over the rules, and the evidence is vectors, fuzzing against the landed code and exhaustive runs of the size arithmetic against the marshaler.

```text
R1 Total       extract_file and extract_mail return for every byte string and every path, with no error; a
               message gives at least one document
R2 A function  their result depends on the path's bytes, the content's bytes and 11.2.1's tables alone: no
               clock, locale, map order, integer width, build leg or library parser enters it
R3 Bounded     time is linear in the input; the fields hold at most 3.6 times the input's bytes plus a
               constant
R4 One pass    the one-pass form of 11.2.8 computes the same function in fixed memory
R5 Kept out    no byte of an entity's body that M4 or M6 stops at reaches a field, and no header field but
               Subject, From, To and Cc of the message's own block
R6 Idempotent  N1-N5 give the same value when applied twice; nothing else is claimed to be

Z-A Exact      a body built from an admissible content is exactly its size
Z-B Requests   every request within Z4's caps is admissible
Z-C Progress   a reply always has an admissible form, and one with at least one hit when there is a hit
Z-D One form   a message has one body, so a pad of zeros hides nothing
```

**R1.** Every rule ends in an "otherwise" that takes input as text or drops it, and no rule can fail: H5 passes over a line, W2 leaves a word as written, C2 leaves bytes, M2 and M6 give nothing, T2 stops, T3 and X6 copy a byte, E4 copies. Every scan moves forward: each step consumes at least one byte, or, in W5, moves the position 2 on. The searches that run ahead (X1's "-->", X3's '>', X5's end tag, a line's LF) either find their mark and resume after it or end that value. A message always reaches D4, which gives one chunk even for an empty text.

**R2.** Read the rules for what they take in. Bytes compare as bytes or under `lower`; the only sets of bytes are white, blank, letters, digits and the base64 alphabet. Numbers: a section is at most 999,999,999 and a numeric reference is held at 0x110000, so both fit 31 bits; everything else is a length. P3 keeps pieces by name and section, the first of each counting, and P5 reads them by name and by ascending section, so no order of a map is ever read. The tables are pinned and checked: the Unicode and x/text versions at start by `indexLinkedTables` (landed), the 2,231 references and 228 labels by the vector files, the block tags by vector `x-block-list`, the 40 decoders by the `c-sweep-` vectors over one sample. C3 is the one rule defined by reference to code, x/text v0.43.0's decoders, which normalizer 1 already makes part of the format; over 3,000 random inputs each, none of the 40 returned an error.

**R3.** Sizes by stage: base64 gives 3 bytes for 4 and quoted-printable never more than it takes; a charset decoder gives at most 3 bytes a byte (measured at exactly 3.00 over those random inputs, a single byte becoming U+FFFD or a three-byte character); removing tags only removes; a reference never grows except `&nLt;` and `&nGt;`, 5 bytes giving 6. So a part's text is at most 3.6 times its bytes, and a header value's at most 3 times its 16,384. Time: every stage is a scan with bounded lookahead (11.2.8's table), and the whole-value form reads a part once per multipart level around it, at most 17 times. W5's failed starts cost in all at most three times the value's length: each reads no further than the third '?' after it, and every later start holds a '?'.

**R4.** By 11.2.8's table: every rule decides on the bytes it has plus a lookahead that the table bounds, and the three unbounded lookaheads of 11.1 C are gone (H4 and H6 cap a value, B1 caps a delimiter line, T3 caps a soft break's blank run). This is argued here and not run: SEARCH-M10-44 builds the form, and its fuzz target, equality with the whole-value form on every input and every split of it into writes, is the check.

**R5.** M4 and M6 return before any rule reads the body. H6 is called with seven names and no other: four for the message, three for each entity. Vectors `m-order`, `m-text-attachment`, `b-preamble-epilogue` and `h-transport-headers` carry a canary where it must not be read, and the landed `FuzzIndexExtractAttachment` keeps its claim.

**R6.** SEARCH-M10-03's fuzz target holds N1-N5 idempotent over every code point and 22 million strings, with QD-256's map. Extraction is not idempotent and nothing applies it twice. N7 is not either: a document's text has doubled spaces between fields that N5 would fold, and nothing normalizes a document's text again.

**Z-A.** Let gap = size - content. If 131 <= gap <= 16,386 then L = gap - 3 lies in 128 to 16,383, whose varint is two bytes, and 1 + 2 + L = gap. If 16,388 <= gap <= 2,097,155 then L = gap - 4 lies in 16,384 to 2,097,151, three bytes, and 1 + 3 + L = gap. `pad` is the last field and no other field's encoding depends on it, so the body is the content's bytes followed by those gap bytes.

**Z-B.** With every field at its cap and every integer at its widest, the marshaler gives a page-0 request 3,778 B: 2,432 for 64 repos, 515 for the query, 771 for the filters, 60 for the rest. A later page is at most 36 B. Both are under 3,885 = 4,016 - 131, and no request's gap can be 16,387.

**Z-C.** With 64 coverage rows and every integer at its widest, a reply without hits is at most 7,578 B, and one hit at its caps adds at most 3,248 B. So the content with no hit is at most 7,578 and with one hit at most 10,826, both under 16,253 = 16,384 - 131, the tightest size. Neither can be size - 16,387, which is below zero at one step and at least 16,381 at more. Z6's loop therefore ends at k >= 1 when there is a hit and at k = 0 otherwise. A failure's 90 B is admissible at every size: its gap is 16,294 or more at one step and past 16,388 at more.

**Z-D.** Z8 (d) accepts a body only if marshaling its parsed message gives it back, and the marshaler has one output for a message with no unknown field. So two accepted bodies that parse alike are equal, an accepted body has one `pad` and it is the body's tail, and (e) reads every byte of it.

**What was run**, on 2026-11-10 with go1.27.3 on darwin/arm64 and x/text v0.43.0, against the landed extractors (`evs_index_extract_mail.go` at 7c06b9a, `sidecartest/search_oracle_extract.go` at 92d7ab7) and `rpc_search.go` at 42d965f. The harness is a reference implementation written from 11.2's rules, the cases, and the size checks. It lives outside the repository, in `.stack/scratch/details-11/`, since this section changes no code, and neither extractor's author should read it: the two are written from the rules, apart, and what they share is the vectors. 11.6 says which task rebuilds each check as a test.

```text
vectors          372 cases through the reference: 329 messages, 43 files, 368 documents. 324 carry a field
                 or a verdict written by hand, and all 324 matched. The landed normalizer and the oracle's
                 give the same text for every document of every case.
landed index     differs from the reference on 32 vectors, each named in 11.7; equal on the other 340, the six
                 of testdata/index/extract/ among them, and on those its rows and key counts, through
                 IndexDocument.prepare, are the vectors' for all 336 documents
landed oracle    differs on 41: those 32, where it reads as the index does, and the 9 of 11.1 A
completeness     the reference, switched to read as the landed index at each place 11.7 lists and nowhere
                 else, equals indexExtractMail over 1,283,751 fuzz executions seeded with the vectors, and
                 indexExtractFile over 176,041 executions: the list of changes is whole, to that confidence
a second reading the rules of 11.2 written out again from this text, in Python with none of Go's libraries,
                 give the vectors' fields and verdicts for 335 of the 372. The other 37 pass through an
                 x/text decoder that reading does not have. Where Python's own table was tried in its place
                 it differed on four: x/text reads 0x80 to 0x9F of ISO 8859-2, -5 and -15 as U+FFFD, and
                 two code points of KOI8-U otherwise, which is why C3 names the module and the c-sweep
                 vectors pin it.
pad              every pad length 1 to 70,000 through the marshaler: the gaps it cannot fill, 0 to 65,536, are
                 1, 2, 130 and 16,387, and Z2 gives the marshaler's length for every other gap from 131
rule             for each of the five sizes and every content 0 to the size: admissible implies sizable; the
                 rule refuses 128 contents a size that a shorter pad would have sized (gaps 0 and 3 to 129)
requests         166,725 bodies: every query length 0 to 512 with every repo count 0 to 64, with no filters and
                 with filters of 3, 126, 127 and 768 B; each exactly 4,016 B, parsed back equal, and Z8 (d) true
replies          60,000 seeded random replies at 1 to 4 steps with 0 to 25 hits to give: each exactly its size,
                 Z8 (d) true, the kept hits a prefix, at least one kept whenever there was one; 1,058 held hits
                 back
the gap          replies built to sit on it: 6 hits of 16,381 B at two steps, 11 of 32,765 B at three, 17 of
                 49,149 B at four; each is built with one hit fewer, and with one more when one more is waiting
refusals         a body of the right size with a non-zero pad byte, an unknown field, pad twice, a zero
                 written out, two fields out of order or a varint one byte too long is refused by Z8; so is
                 one of the wrong size
the one encoding 40,000 seeded bodies from the builders, requests and replies, are each accepted by a walker of
                 Z9's rule of bytes that calls no marshaler, which refuses the malformed ones as Z8 (d) does
```

### 11.4 Cost

Measured on the same host, one run each. "Landed" is `indexExtractMail` as it stands, which holds everything at once. The last column is what it allocated, as a multiple of the message.

```text
message                                           size        extract   normalize, keys   documents   allocated
49 KiB, two alternatives, quoted-printable        49,401 B    0.5 ms    1.2 ms            1           9.5 x
50 MiB, one 49 MiB base64 attachment              52.7 MB     8 ms      0.5 ms            1           0.0 x
50 MiB, all one base64 text/plain part            53.1 MB     64 ms     1,117 ms          38          2.5 x
2 MiB of windows-1252 HTML, every byte growing    2.1 MB      9 ms      50 ms             2           8.1 x
```

- **Time.** Normalizing and collecting keys runs at 30 to 35 MB/s here and is 10 to 20 times extraction's cost on text; an attachment costs a scan for delimiter lines, about 6 GB/s. The rules of 11.2 add nothing that shows: the reference's plain loops for base64 and quoted-printable ran the worst case at 98 MB/s, three times faster than the normalizer that follows them. A phone taken at a fifth of this host's speed extracts and normalizes a typical message in under 10 ms, and the 50 MiB all-text message, the largest §15's limits admit, in about 6 s: 9 MB/s, against §11.15's floor of 5 on mobile.
- **Memory, whole-value form.** 2.5 to 10 times the message, as measured: the message, each part decoded, each part again in UTF-8, the joined text. For a 50 MiB message that is over 130 MB, past even the daemon's 128 MiB budget (§18). So the one-pass form is what every writer runs once it lands, and the whole-value form stays for tests and the oracle.
- **Memory, one-pass form.** 11.2.8's table summed: the line window 1 KiB, sixteen boundaries 16 KiB, the header line being read 16 KiB, one entity's three header values 48 KiB, the message's four joined values 64 KiB, a soft break's blank run 1 KiB and under 1 KiB for the rest: at most 150 KiB, whatever the message. That is all extraction adds. What dominates is not its own: the normalizer's buffers and the key collector, a 2 MiB bitmap and up to 1 MiB of touched words (SEARCH-M10-03, landed), with a document's key set beside them when its entry is built. One collector is live at a time (11.2.8, point 3), and whether a writer's peak fits §11.15's 4 MiB on the iOS app is FS-77's to measure, as before. The message itself stays in storage and is read once, front to back; a file is read twice when its title is not near its start (point 4).
- **Index size.** Extraction sets how many documents a version has: one per MiB of extracted text. Reading every alternative roughly doubles a typical message's text, and changes its key set little, since both alternatives hold the same words. The most text a message gives is three times its size (R3): 50 MiB of 8-bit bytes that each decode to a three-byte character are 150 MiB of text and 150 documents, each skipped past 512 KiB of key set (D6), so at most 75 MiB of entries, which §11.14's document and sniff rows already allow. D6's shard test (amended 2026-11-12, QD-760) only lowers that: a kept document has at most 206,438 keys. The test is one pass over a key set the writer already holds, an addition and two comparisons a key, and it allocates nothing.
- **Code size.** The reference table is about 32 KB packed (16.6 KB of names, 6.4 KB of values, offsets) on every leg that links the index, `sidecar_http` included. The standard library's copy of the same list stays linked while `mail_parse_text.go` calls `html`; if that file takes the extractor's decoder (11.7), the copy can leave wherever nothing else links `html`, and the change is then about nil.
- **Padding.** A request is one size computation and one marshal of 4 KiB. A reply is at most 21 size computations and one marshal of 16 to 64 KiB, well under a millisecond. Z8 (d) is one more marshal and a comparison per body received. The rule gives up at most 131 B of a body, 0.8% of a step, and the gap costs one hit of one page only when a content lands on one value in 16,384.

### 11.5 Failure modes

```text
malformed mail          read by 11.2.7's table. Nothing is refused, so no message is unsearchable for its
                        damage: the index holds what a lenient reader would show. Two devices read it alike (R2).
mail built to split     an input chosen so two honest builds disagree would turn the readers' check on an honest
  two devices           writer. Under R2 there is none; before SEARCH-M10-42 and -43 land there are the classes
                        of 11.1 A and B, so no index is written outside tests until both have landed.
a cut message           its last part runs to the end (B4); base64 decodes to its last whole or partial group
                        (T2); a last '=' is a soft break (T3); an open tag or script drops the tail (X7)
huge parts              time and memory as 11.4. An attachment of any size costs a scan. Text is chunked (D4),
                        and a chunk of noise is skipped (D6). The one-pass form never holds a part.
a document past a shard (amended 2026-11-12, QD-760) a chunk within KeySetMax that alone would not fit a
                        shard is skipped (D6): no entry, a tombstone where it was indexed before, and nothing
                        alarms, since every device skips it alike. It is not searchable. Before the amendment
                        it was kept, and the merge that met it failed closed, so its bucket stopped merging.
a huge header           a field past 16,384 B is cut (H4, H6): its tail is not indexed. A header block of any
                        length is read, each line of no interest discarded as it arrives.
unknown charset         bytes as they are (C2): ASCII words are found, and the rest reads as U+FFFD, which N5
                        folds into a space. No guess is made, since a guess is a table of its own to pin.
wrong charset label     decoded as labelled: that part's text is indexed as the wrong characters and its true
                        words are not found in it. Another alternative, if it is labelled right, is found. An
                        HTML part's own <meta charset> is not read.
another decoder        C3 means x/text v0.43.0's tables. They are not every library's: its ISO 8859 decoders
                        read 0x80 to 0x9F as U+FFFD where others give C1 controls. A writer on another
                        decoder fails the c-sweep vectors.
iso-2022-kr, hz-gb-2312 the Encoding Standard decodes these to one U+FFFD. Here they pass as bytes (C2), so the
                        ASCII in them is found.
a word a line breaks    normalizer 1 turns a line break into a space, so a CJK word broken by a hard line break
                        is two words. Quoted-printable's soft breaks are joined (T3). format=flowed's are not
                        (RFC 3676, DelSp): extractor 1 reads no such parameter. An HTML alternative, where there
                        is one, holds the word whole.
damaged markup          a quote left open inside a tag takes the text after it into the tag, up to the next quote
                        of its kind (X3); an open comment or script takes the rest of the part (X7). A plain
                        alternative, where there is one, still holds the words.
a forwarded message     a message/rfc822 part is an attachment: its name is indexed and its text is not (M6)
signed, encrypted mail  multipart/signed is read through, its signature part giving its name; multipart/
                        encrypted and pkcs7-mime give their parts' names alone
a writer on old rules   a build from before SEARCH-M10-42 writes entries that differ on the classes of 11.1; a
                        reader with the text reports index_mismatch and uses its own. After the format freezes
                        at M10's exit, any change to a rule of 11.2 is extractor 2 and a rebuild beside i1
                        (§11.14's rebuild row).
other tables            a build linking another Unicode or x/text writes nothing and reads status update (landed)
a request over a cap    never sent: the search stays on the device (Z5)
a hit over a cap        the builder leaves it out, as a receiver would (Z8 f), and counts it; building a reply
                        cannot fail, so no small Error follows a parsed request
a body not its one      INVALID from an indexer; no reply to a requester, which fails over (Z8)
  encoding
```

### 11.6 The test plan

**The conformance vectors**, `sidecar/testdata/index/conformance/`:

```text
mail.json      329 messages, each with its documents: fields 1, 2, 3 and 5 before normalization, the normalized
               text, the key count and the row. By rule group, a vector counting once for each group it
               pins: header block 28, encoded words 42, parameters 36, charsets 73 (40 of them one sample
               through each encoding), the walk 35, multipart bodies 22, transfer encodings 34, tags 39,
               references 26, documents and chunks 21.
file.json      43 files, 10 of them binary: 38 on the sniff, the marks and the title, 7 on fields and chunks.
               Each text file's documents: fields 4 and 5, the text, the key count and the row.
entities.json  the 2,231 named references
charsets.json  the 228 labels and their 40 encodings
sizes.json     85 rows of (size, content): sized or not, the pad's length and its varint's; and 7 whole
               bodies, each with its content bytes and the SHA-256 of the body
skip.json      (amended 2026-11-12, QD-760; the fix track writes it) D6's shard test: rows of a key set given
               as runs (first key, count, step), a row's length, lone(d) and the verdict. The empty set; 1,
               63, 64, 65 and 129 keys; each value of p at a block's first key and at its second; an offset
               at each VByte width; keys 0 to n - 1 at n = 199,608 and 199,609 under a 36 B row (1,032,192
               kept, 1,032,197 skipped), and the first again under a 37 B row, skipped; steps of 64, 256 and
               65,536; and a set past KeySetMax, skipped
```

- **Their form.** A vector's `input` is its parts in order, each `t` (text) or `x` (hex) and an optional repeat count `n`; its `path` is text, or `path_x` in hex when the path is not UTF-8. A value is `t`, `x`, or `len` and `sha256` when it is long. A document's `fields` are by number, an absent one being empty. Each file's `about` says the same.
- **How they were made.** The inputs were written by hand, one or more for each rule and each "otherwise" of 11.2, and include every example of 11.1 and the six cases `testdata/index/extract/` already pins. The outputs come from the reference implementation of 11.3. For 324 of them the expected field or verdict was also written by hand and compared, and where the landed extractor already agrees, 340 vectors, its rows and key counts were compared too.
- **How they are kept.** They are data, with their inputs inside them. No implementation rewrites them: `SIDECAR_WRITE_VECTORS` does not reach this directory. A change to a rule of 11.2 changes this section, `INDEX-FORMAT.md`, the vectors and both implementations in one change, by hand.
- **How both implementations pass them.** Each runs every vector through its own entry points and compares every value the vector gives: `indexExtractMail` and `indexExtractFile` with `IndexDocument.prepare` in the root (`evs_index_conformance_test.go`, SEARCH-M10-42), and `searchOracleMailDocuments` and `searchOracleFileDocuments` in `sidecartest` (`search_oracle_conformance_test.go`, SEARCH-M10-43). A value given as `len` and `sha256` is compared that way. Each also checks its own copy of the reference table against `entities.json`, name for name, and that its label lookup gives `charsets.json`'s encoding for each label and nothing for a label outside it.
- **Every leg.** SEARCH-M10-41's runner reproduces `testdata/index/` on each leg, this directory included. The 32-bit legs matter here: P3's sections and E1's numbers are the places an integer's width could have shown.

**The cross-implementation check** (SEARCH-M10-43, under `sidecar_testhooks`): `FuzzExtractOracleEqualsIndex` in `sidecartest` takes any bytes as a message and as a file, and requires the oracle's documents and the index's, reached through the seam `sidecar.TestHookIndexExtract`, to be equal: count, fields before normalization, rows. Its seeds are every vector under 64 KiB. `TestExtractOracleEqualsIndexOnCorpus` does the same over `SearchCorpus`'s generated mail and notes. The oracle's import check stays: the seam is called from the test file, never from an oracle file.

**Fuzz targets.**

```text
FuzzIndexExtractMail, -File        landed: total; fields within 4 x the input + 1,024 B, which R3's 3.6 keeps;
                                   seeds gain every vector
FuzzIndexExtractAttachment         landed: no attachment byte in a field (R5)
FuzzExtractOracleEqualsIndex       new: the two implementations agree on everything (R2)
FuzzIndexExtractStreamEqualsWhole  new, SEARCH-M10-44: for any input and any split of it into writes, the
                                   one-pass form's keys and rows equal the whole-value form's (R4)
FuzzSearchRequestBody, -ReplyBody  §22.6's target, SEARCH-M10-31: parsing is total and memory-bounded; a body is
                                   accepted only if Z8 holds; an accepted body marshals back to itself
```

**Unit tests for sizes** (`search_remote_wire_test.go`, SEARCH-M10-31), each a top-level test and each one of 11.3's runs:

```text
TestSearchPadFillsEveryGapButFour     every pad length 1 to 70,000 through the marshaler; Z2 against it
TestSearchAdmissibleIsSound           every content at the five sizes
TestSearchCapBounds                   the marshaler's sizes at the caps: 3,778, 36, 7,578, 3,248, 90
TestSearchRequestSizes                every query length 0-512 with every repo count 0-64, filters none and at
                                      3, 127, 128 and 768 B
TestSearchReplySizes                  seeded random replies at each step count; the kept hits a prefix
TestSearchReplyOnTheGap               the built replies of 6, 11 and 17 hits at two, three and four steps
TestSearchBodyIsItsOneEncoding        Z8's refusals: a non-zero pad, an unknown field, pad twice, a long varint,
                                      a zero written out, fields out of order, a wrong size; and a walker of
                                      Z9 written without the marshaler accepting every body the builders make
TestSearchSizeVectors                 sizes.json, row by row and body by body
```

FS-83's size cases stay as planned (0, 1 and 20 hits, TOO_BROAD, INVALID, CURSOR_EXPIRED, UNSUPPORTED_VERSION) and gain a reply on the gap at two steps. FS-76 gains the vectors' messages in its corpus (11.7).

**Mutants.** Each of these, put back, must fail a vector, and the landed code is the proof that it does: the library's quoted-printable reader (`t-qp-long-line`, `t-qp-control-bytes`), its base64 (`t-base64-unpadded`), `html.UnescapeString` (`e-one-digit`, `e-overflow`, `e-two-code-points`), `strings.TrimSpace` and `strings.ToLower` (`h-value-nbsp-stays`, `h-name-ascii-case-only`), `strconv.Atoi` (`p-section-signed`), no HeaderMax (`h-cap-line`), no LineWindow (`b-line-one-past-window`), no digest default (`m-digest-default`). For sizes: a pad computed by trial that stops at a gap (`TestSearchReplyOnTheGap`), and a receiver without Z8 (d) (`TestSearchBodyIsItsOneEncoding`).

**D6's shard test** (amended 2026-11-12, QD-760). The fix track's tests, the index's in the root and the oracle's in `sidecartest`, by different authors (D-TEST-14):

```text
skip.json, both sides           each implementation's own lone(d) and verdict equal every row's
TestLoneShardBoundsTheEncoder   root: for skip.json's kept rows and generated sets, the encoder's length of a
                                shard holding the document alone is lone(d) - 33 at the widest header, version
                                and time, and less at every other; a kept document's lone shard is never refused
TestADocumentPastAShardIsSkipped
                                root, through prepare and the one-pass form: 1 MiB of letters drawn by a fixed
                                generator from the BMP's two-byte and three-byte letters has a key set within
                                KeySetMax and is skipped, in a file and in a message's body; 1 MiB of base64
                                is kept; a version skipped where its key was indexed before is a tombstone,
                                and one never indexed leaves nothing
TestExtractOracleEqualsIndexOnCorpus
                                gains the generated chunk and a kept one beside it, and compares which
                                documents are skipped; TestHookIndexExtract returns that for each document
FuzzIndexLoneShard              root: for any key set and row the codec accepts, lone(d) is at least 33 B above
                                the encoder's length of the lone shard at a fuzzed header, version and time
```

Mutants: D6 with KeySetMax alone fails `TestADocumentPastAShardIsSkipped` and skip.json's boundary rows; ShardLone at 0 fails the 199,609 row; a p that does not reset at a block's first key, an offset counted in keys and a list offset of j each fail a named row.

### 11.7 Implementation notes, task by task

Order: SEARCH-M10-42 and SEARCH-M10-43 at once, by different authors (D-TEST-14). SEARCH-M10-31 at once; it shares nothing with them. SEARCH-M10-44 after SEARCH-M10-42. SEARCH-M10-36 after SEARCH-M10-42 and SEARCH-M10-43, with its other needs. All are the data lane's. Entries for the three new tasks are in `.stack/plan/proposals/details-11-tasks.md`.

**SEARCH-M10-31, remote search's wire** (held; M; its Build line changes). Build Z1 to Z9 in `search_remote_wire.go`. Proposed names: `searchRemotePadByteCount(bodyByteCount, contentByteCount int) (int, bool)` is Z2; `searchRemoteAdmissible` Z3; `searchRemoteBuildRequest` Z5; `searchRemoteBuildReply(steps int, hits []*protocol.SearchHit, head func(hitCount int) *protocol.SearchReply) ([]byte, int)` Z6, returning the body and how many hits it took; `searchRemoteFailureReply` Z7; `searchRemoteParseRequest` and `searchRemoteParseReply` Z8, the first returning the status to answer with. Landed code that changes: in `rpc_search.go`, `padSearchReply` loses its loop over five pad lengths and takes its length from `searchRemotePadByteCount`, keeping `errSearchReplySize` for a content that is not admissible; `searchInvalidReply` builds Z7's reply through it, and its output for the landed tests does not change. The plan's "a request over budget splits by repo" goes: under Z4 no request is over budget. Traps: take the content with `proto.Size` after clearing `pad`, never from a previous marshal; `head` must be a pure function of its count, since it is called up to 21 times, and it is where `checked_through_ms` is computed for the hits kept, which is the plan's own trap; apply Z8 (f)'s dropping to the builder's own hits first, so that building cannot fail; in Z8 check the version before (d); a parsed request is never answered with an Error. Tests: 11.6's.

**SEARCH-M10-36, results against the oracle** (held; L; its Needs and corpus change). The schedules are as planned. Its corpus gains every conformance vector under 64 KiB as a document, at fixed days of the 200, and its query set gains terms that only the canonical reading finds: a word a soft line break joins, a name from RFC 2231 sections, a word after a 4,096 B quoted-printable line, a word behind `&#9` and one inside an unpadded base64 tail. So FS-76's "the desktop's hits checked against its own text equal the oracle's" is exercised on the inputs of 11.1, which the generated corpus never reached. It needs SEARCH-M10-42 and SEARCH-M10-43: on the landed extractors those documents fail it, at the nine vectors of 11.1 A.

**SEARCH-M10-42, extractor 1 to the canonical rules** (new; M). The landed code that changes, by file:

```text
evs_index_extract_mail.go  indexSplitMailHeader: names and values by lower and trim of bytes (H5), HeaderMax
                           (H4); the joined values cut (H6)
                           indexDecodeCharset: the label's bytes, and utf-8 and replacement left alone (C1, C2)
                           indexDecodeEncodedWord: base64 by W3, with no skipped CR
                           indexParseMediaValue: lower and trim of bytes; a section is 1-9 digits (P3)
                           indexMultipartParts: LineWindow (B1)
                           indexMimeWalk: a digest's part with no Content-Type is message/rfc822 (M1)
                           indexTransferDecode: selects by T1 and calls the two decoders below
                           the imports of encoding/base64, encoding/hex, mime/quotedprintable and strconv go
evs_index_extract_transfer.go   new: indexBase64Body (T2) and indexQuotedPrintable (T3)
evs_index_extract_html.go  indexStripHtml keeps X1-X7 as landed and ends in indexDecodeReferences (E1-E4); the
                           import of html goes
evs_index_extract_entities.go   new: the 2,231 names, generated from entities.json and checked against it
evs_index_sniff.go         indexSniff: S3
evs_index_document.go      no change of bytes: field 4 is already the title, a space and the path. Its comment
                           and evs_index_extract_mail.go's lose "pending question".
protocol/INDEX-FORMAT.md   Extractor 1 and Documents become 11.8's text
```

The 32 vectors the landed code fails are its list of work: `h-value-nbsp-stays`, `h-name-ascii-case-only`, `h-cap-line`, `h-cap-fold`, `h-cap-join`, `w-b-carriage-return`, `p-section-signed`, `p-section-ten-digits`, `m-digest-default`, `b-line-one-past-window`, `b-line-past-window`, `t-base64-stops-at-garbage`, `t-base64-unpadded`, `t-base64-one-pad-of-two`, `t-base64-two-left`, `t-qp-control-bytes`, `t-qp-long-line`, `t-qp-trailing-whitespace`, `t-qp-cr-without-lf`, `t-qp-padding-past-window`, `c-label-not-ascii`, `c-replacement-passes`, `c-replacement-empty`, `c-sweep-replacement`, `e-two-code-points`, `e-one-digit`, `e-one-digit-at-end`, `e-no-digits`, `e-overflow`, `s-utf-8-mark`, `s-utf-8-mark-only`, `s-utf-8-mark-twice`. Five of them (the three `h-cap-`, `t-qp-trailing-whitespace` and `s-utf-8-mark-twice`) change a field's bytes and not its entry. `testdata/index/extract/vectors.json` keeps its bytes: the reference gives the landed output for all six. It also adds the seam `TestHookIndexExtract` under `sidecar_testhooks`, which returns each document's chunk number, its five text fields as the normalizer is given them and its row's values. Traps: write the decoders as the rules read, byte loops with no regular expression and no library decoder, since the point is that nothing outside this repository can change them; the table is data, so generate it and test it against the file rather than typing it; `lower` and `trim` are of bytes everywhere, and `bytes.EqualFold`, `strings.ToLower` and `strings.TrimSpace` have no place in these files; C1 is `htmlindex.Get` behind the check that every byte of the trimmed label is 0x21 to 0x7E, and `htmlindex.Name` tells utf-8 and replacement from the rest; keep `indexDropsMarks` and the normalizer untouched.

**SEARCH-M10-43, the oracle's extractor to the canonical rules** (new; M; another author than SEARCH-M10-42's). `sidecartest/search_oracle_extract.go` is brought to 11.2 from this section and `INDEX-FORMAT.md`, sharing nothing with the index: its own base64, quoted-printable and reference decoders and its own generated copy of the table (`search_oracle_entities.go`). The 41 vectors it fails are the index's 32 and the 9 where it read differently: `x-script-end-name` (X5), `t-base64-nbsp-stops` (T2), `w-charset-with-space` (W2), `w-nbsp-between` and `w-cr-between` (W6), `p-sections-without-zero`, `p-sections-empty-fall-through` and `p-sections-repeat` (P3, P5), `b-unterminated` (B4). `searchOracleDocument` keeps its fields before normalization, for the cross check. It adds `search_oracle_conformance_test.go` and the cross-implementation fuzz target and corpus test of 11.6. Trap: the oracle may not take the index's table or decoders to save work; `TestSearchOracleImportsNoIndexCode` must keep failing on that.

**SEARCH-M10-44, extraction in one pass** (new; L). Build 11.2.8 in new files (`evs_index_extract_stream.go` and beside it): a message is written to it front to back in pieces of any size, and it hands each finished document to the caller as its key set and row, never as text; a file is read through an `io.ReaderAt`. The whole-value functions stay, as the form the vectors and the oracle are compared with and the form the fuzz target holds this one to. Writers call the one-pass form on every host once it lands (SEARCH-M10-13 and SEARCH-M10-14, which problem 1 holds). Tests: every conformance vector, written in one piece, byte by byte and in random pieces; `FuzzIndexExtractStreamEqualsWhole`; a generated 50 MiB message of each of 11.4's shapes with the heap sampled at each document, its growth over the normalizer's own staying under 256 KiB whatever the message. Traps: hold a line break back until the next line is known not to be a delimiter; test a line against the boundaries outermost first; never buffer a part to learn its length; one key bitmap at a time, the 256 B overlap replayed into the next document.

**The fix track for QD-760, extraction side** (amended 2026-11-12, QD-760). D6's shard test in the index, with the format file and the vectors. The oracle's half is a second track by another author (D-TEST-14), and 11.6's corpus case lands with whichever of the two is second. Section 1.7 has the merge side. Landed code that changes:

```text
evs_index_document.go       indexKeySetSkipped(keys) becomes indexDocumentSkipped(keys, row, settings): the
                            key set's encoding against KeySetMax first, then lone(d) against ShardBody.
                            IndexDocument.prepare builds and checks the row before the test, where it tested
                            before the row existed; a skipped result still holds no key set and no row
evs_index_lone.go           new: indexLoneShardByteCount(rowByteCount, keys, settings), D6's sum in one pass
                            over the keys, with no call into the shard encoder
evs_index_extract_stream.go its call at a finished document follows prepare's
evs_index_settings.go       IndexFormatSettings gains ShardLoneByteCount, 128 (QD-702)
sidecartest/search_oracle_normalize.go
                            the oracle's own sum beside searchOracleKeySetByteCount, written from 11.2.3 and
                            INDEX-FORMAT.md and sharing nothing with the index (the second track)
protocol/INDEX-FORMAT.md    D6 as 11.2.3 has it, a Limits row for ShardLone, 11.2.7's row and 1.8's two
                            sentences
testdata/index/conformance/skip.json
                            11.6's rows, with its `about`
```

Traps: the row's length is that of the row as its entry encodes it, in its own root, so `ur/index`'s 16 B ref_id counts; the sum runs over the key set as the collector gives it, ascending and distinct; KeySetMax is tested first, so a set of millions of keys costs no pass; a journal unit (1.2.6) holds what `prepare` returned, so a skipped document's unit is its tombstone or nothing, as before; and the format is not frozen until M10's exit, so no index outside tests holds an entry in the gap and nothing migrates.

**Tasks not held that this touches.** SEARCH-M10-41's runner needs no change to reach the new directory; its report should name the 32-bit legs for it. SEARCH-M10-06 and SEARCH-M10-07 are drafted, and their extract files are finished by SEARCH-M10-42 and SEARCH-M10-43. SEARCH-M10-32 calls `searchRemoteBuildReply` with its own `head`, and answers every failure after parsing through `searchRemoteFailureReply`. Of the landed pads, the one that changes is `padSearchReply`, with SEARCH-M10-31. An index document's own pad, normalizer 1's one space each side of a field (`indexFieldPad`, N7), and a shard's keyed pad and a rewrite's zero pad (`evs_index_pad.go`) are as landed.

**The mail lane's parser.** MAIL-M7-11's `MailParseMessage` (`mail_parse.go`, `mail_parse_text.go`) is a third reading of a message, for `i/` entries and their 200 B snippet (§15.7). It is MAIL-FORMAT.md's and no index byte: FI-22 does not reach it, and a phone that confirms a hit from a snippet (§11.14's confirm row) is reading a display field. Its comment says it reads charsets and HTML as extractor 1 does, so that a snippet says what search indexes. After SEARCH-M10-42 that holds only if it calls the extractor's functions, which are in its package: `indexStripHtml` for `mailHtmlText` and `indexDecodeCharset` for `mailDecodeCharset`. That is the edge lane's change, small, and no task here waits on it (question `details-11-mail-snippet-reading`).

### 11.8 Proposed DESIGN.md text

**§11.14, Documents, the extract row.** Replace the row: "extract   extractor 1, every byte of which protocol/INDEX-FORMAT.md fixes and testdata/index/conformance/ pins; it calls no library parser, reads damaged input by rule and refuses none; mail: the message's own Subject, From, To and Cc values with RFC 2047 words decoded (fields 1, 2 and 3, To before Cc), and in field 5, in the message's order and joined by one space, each part's name and each text/plain and text/html part's text, MIME-decoded (RFC 2045, 2231), HTML with its tags, scripts and styles removed and its character references decoded; every alternative is read, an attachment gives its name alone, a message/rfc822 part is one, and multiparts are read 16 deep; never transport headers, attachment bytes or base64; files: the title is the first line holding a letter or a number, without its heading marks, at most 80 B; field 4 is the title, a space and the path, and field 5 the text; records: §16.8's mapping of an entry's sealed body; every chunk of a document carries its fields 1-4; the extractor's id is in every file header".

**§11.14, Documents, the sniff row.** After "or it opens with a UTF-16 byte-order mark and is decoded": "; a UTF-8 byte-order mark is dropped".

**§11.14, Files and format, the determinism row.** After "no clock, randomness or library-version input": "; extraction's base64, quoted-printable, character-reference, header and multipart readings are the format's own rules, and no library's parser is part of them".

**§11.14, search.proto.** `SearchFilters`: "// <= 768 B as encoded in a SearchRequest". `SearchCoverage.chain`: "// <= 32 B". `SearchHit.correction`: "// near: the corrected term, <= 256 B". The `pad` comments stand.

**§11.14, the sizes row.** After "failures after parsing included;": "a body is the one deterministic encoding of its message, pad last; every other field stops at the body's size less 131 B, so pad's length takes two bytes or three, and a reply whose other fields would leave exactly 16,387 B returns the most hits, at most 20, that leave another gap;".

**§11.14, the status row.** INVALID's list becomes: "(a wrong size, a body that is not its message's one encoding or holds a field this version does not know, a non-zero pad, a query over 512 B or 16 terms, over 64 repos, an id of the wrong length, steps outside 1 to 4, filters over 768 B or malformed)". UNSUPPORTED_VERSION gains: "judged before the encoding, so a later version's fields are not INVALID".

**§11.15.** A row: "Index extraction | one pass in fixed memory on app hosts: at most 150 KiB beyond normalizer 1's buffers and one key bitmap, whatever the message".

**§11.17, D-EVS-44.** After "byte-exact determinism": ", extraction included: extractor 1 is specified to the byte and calls no library parser".

**§11.17, D-EVS-59.** After "failures after parsing included": ", each body the one encoding of its message".

**§16.10, filters.** "A remote request carries at most 768 B of encoded filters; a search with more stays on the device, with fallback reason none." (QD-215, restated where §16.10 lists them.)

**§22.12, D-TEST-14.** Add: "The oracle's extractor and the index's are held to one set of conformance vectors and to equality under a fuzz target, since on damaged mail two readings of the same rule are the likeliest way for the two to differ."

**§22.6.** The every-body target's `SearchRequest` and `SearchReply` line gains: "a body that is not its message's one encoding is refused". A line for extraction: "**Extractor 1** (messages and files): total; fields within four times the input; the index, the oracle and the one-pass form equal on every input; no attachment byte in a field."

**§22.9's Index determinism row and §22.12's D-TEST-15.** `testdata/index/`'s list gains "extraction (mail, files, the character-reference table, the charset labels) and search body sizes".

**§22.8, FS-76.** After "MIME with base64, quoted-printable and HTML parts": ", and the conformance vectors' damaged messages". **FS-83.** After "UNSUPPORTED_VERSION": ", and a two-step reply whose content sits on the 16,387 B gap".

**§22.8, FI-22.** "a function of its format version, normalization version, extractor version and inputs alone".

**protocol/INDEX-FORMAT.md** (SEARCH-M10-42 writes it; `design-records` need not). Its Extractor 1 and Documents sections become 11.2.1's constants and tables and the rules D1-D6, S1-S4, H1-H6, W1-W6, P1-P6, C1-C3, M1-M6, B1-B4, T1-T3, X1-X7 and E1-E4 as written here, with 11.2.7's table. Normalizer 1 gains the clarifications under 11.2.2. "What this file adds" gains a row for each reading 11.9 lists.

**Amended 2026-11-12, QD-760.** §11.14, Documents, the sniff row: for "a chunk whose key set would encode past 512 KiB, which nearly every query would match, is skipped" read "a chunk whose key set would encode past 512 KiB, which nearly every query would match, or that alone would not fit a shard by protocol/INDEX-FORMAT.md's D6, is skipped". §22.8, FS-79: for "chunks whose key set would pass 512 KiB" read "chunks whose key set would pass 512 KiB or that alone would not fit a shard". protocol/INDEX-FORMAT.md, in the fix track's change (11.7): D6 as 11.2.3 has it with lone(d)'s definition, a Limits row "ShardLone 128 B what D6 counts for the header, doc_key, version and time of a shard holding one document", and 11.2.7's added row.

Nothing server-visible changes: no column, key, object family or proto field (I-18), and `search.proto`'s fields are sealed end to end.

### 11.9 Owner questions

Each is filed under `.stack/questions/`, and the design above is built on its recommendation.

**Extraction's own decoders (`details-11-own-decoders.md`; amends QD-474).** Both implementations call the standard library for base64, quoted-printable, character references, case and whitespace, and what those calls do on damaged input is not stated and can change with a Go release. Options: (1) every such reading is a rule of the format, as 11.2 has them, with HTML's reference table in the repository: about 400 lines in each implementation and some 32 KB of table on the legs that index; a Go release can no longer change an index, and four defects go (a quoted-printable part cut at a 4,096 B line or a control byte, a base64 tail lost, `&#9` unread, two of HTML's names unread); (2) keep the calls, and make the Go release part of extractor 1's identity, recorded in headers: any release that touches those packages is a new extractor and a rebuild of every index, and the defects stay; (3) keep the calls and write down what they do today: the rules then describe one release's accidents, the 32-bit sum among them. Recommended: 1. It replaces three sentences of QD-474: references are E1-E4 and not `html.UnescapeString`; a label is read as bytes; `replacement` labels pass as bytes.

**Extraction's limits (`details-11-extraction-bounds.md`).** Three readings need unbounded lookahead, so no one-pass extractor in fixed memory can be exact without a limit on each. Options: (1) HeaderMax 16,384 B and LineWindow 1,024 B as 11.2.1 has them: a header value's tail past 16 KiB is not indexed, where fields 1-3 keep 1,024 normalized bytes anyway, and a delimiter line or soft line break with over 1 KiB of trailing blanks is read as text; no honest message meets either; (2) no limits: exact on any input, and an app host then holds the largest header value or line in memory, up to the message's 50 MiB, or reads the message from storage more than once; (3) larger limits, 65,536 B and 4,096 B: the same shape at four times the memory, about 600 KiB, for inputs no mailer writes. Recommended: 1.

**A search body's one encoding (`details-11-body-encoding.md`).** Options: (1) a receiver refuses a body that is not the deterministic encoding of its message or that holds a field it does not know (Z8 d): the pad check is then complete and a message has one body; a later version's fields must ride a later `search_version`, which the indexer answers UNSUPPORTED_VERSION before it looks at the encoding; (2) accept whatever parses and check the `pad` it parsed: a later requester's fields 13 and 14 can reach an older indexer, which ignores them, and non-zero bytes can ride in a second `pad` or an unknown field, which only the two ends of the sealed session could use. Recommended: 1. The channel is between two devices that already share the session, so the gain is not secrecy; it is that "exactly these bytes" has one meaning, which the size tests and the fuzz target can state.

**Small readings (`details-11-small-readings.md`).** Thirteen readings that change no D- item, listed there by number: a file's UTF-8 mark is dropped (S3); names, labels and encodings compare under ASCII `lower` and only white bytes are trimmed (11.2.1); an unterminated multipart's last part keeps its last line break (B4); of two RFC 2231 pieces of one name, kind and section the first counts, and sections that join to nothing fall through (P3, P5); a section is 1 to 9 digits (P3); base64 decodes a last partial group (T2, W3) and an encoded word's base64 skips nothing; quoted-printable passes control bytes and has no line limit (T3); a numeric reference needs one digit, `&#x;` is text and a number past U+10FFFF is U+FFFD (E1); `SearchHit.correction` is at most 256 B and `SearchCoverage.chain` at most 32 B (Z4); extractor 1 keeps its number (11.2); a digest's part with no Content-Type is message/rfc822 and so not entered (M1); the block-tag list stays QD-474's 44 names, so `title`, `body`, `caption` and `option` leave no space (X4); format=flowed is not read, so its soft line breaks stay breaks (11.5). Options: accept all, or correct any by number. Recommended: accept all.

**The mail snippet's reading (`details-11-mail-snippet-reading.md`; for the edge lane, not the owner).** `mail_parse_text.go` reads HTML and charsets by extractor 1's rules as they stood, with the library's reference decoder. Options: (1) once SEARCH-M10-42 lands it calls `indexStripHtml` and `indexDecodeCharset`: a snippet keeps saying what search indexes, and the library's reference table can leave the binary; (2) leave it: on damaged HTML a snippet and the index can read a reference differently, which breaks no invariant. Recommended: 1.

**Existing questions this section answers.**

- `search-m10-05-extractor-unstated-bytes`: its option 1, and further. Where the two differed, the index's reading is the rule in every case (X5, T2's white bytes, W2, W6, P3, P5, B4). Where both leaned on the library, the rule is 11.2's own (the first question above).
- `search-m10-07-extractor-field-placement`: its option 1 (D2, D3, D4).
- `plan-SEARCH-exact-body-sizes`: decided by the owner as QD-215, which stands. This section makes it exact (Z1-Z7), adds the receiver's rule (Z8, Z9) and the two caps its proof needs (Z4).
- `plan-SEARCH-index-format-bytes` #8 (QD-474, a proposed fill): stands but for the three sentences named above. `plan-SEARCH-cherokee-fold` (QD-256), `plan-SEARCH-small-readings` #1 and #2 (QD-596, QD-387): stand, and N3 and D4 restate them.

## 12. Bridge compiler and NAT engine (§17)

Status: complete (2026-11-11; amended 2026-11-12, QD-761: 12.2.2, 12.2.3, 12.3, 12.5, 12.6, 12.7, 12.8 and 12.9, each place marked; the readers' half of the amendment is built on the recommendation of open question `details-amend-2-late-generation`, and what the amendment leaves to a sidecar that keeps filing is open question `details-amend-2-fold-holds`)

Tasks held until complete: BRIDGE-M4-16, BRIDGE-M4-17, BRIDGE-M6-03, BRIDGE-M6-04.

Models: `sidecar/sidecartest/model/details/BridgeNat.tla` (the engine against the host's NAT), `ShareSign.tla` (a share's signers against removal and revocation) and `BridgeFold.tla` (one body-level verdict at every reader), their configurations (`BridgeNat*.cfg`, `ShareSign*.cfg`, `BridgeFold*.cfg`) and `run-bridge.sh` beside them. Amended 2026-11-12, QD-761: `BridgeVoid.tla` (a body sealed to a generation that does not form), with `BridgeVoid*.cfg` and `run-bridgevoid.sh`. New tasks: `.stack/plan/proposals/details-12-tasks.md` (BRIDGE-M4-23, BRIDGE-M4-24, ACL-M2-17). Questions filed: `.stack/questions/details-12-ledger-in-head.md`, `details-12-unfolded-verdicts.md`, `details-12-start-gate.md`, `details-12-alias-table-pin.md`, `details-12-ratchet-commit.md`. Questions this section answers, each as 12.9 says: `bridge-m4-09-other-client-rows`, `bridge-m4-11-rule-three-tags`. It builds on the answers already given to `plan-BRIDGE-share-pins` (QD-077), `plan-BRIDGE-subject-resolution` (QD-161), `plan-BRIDGE-gate-row-prefixes` (QD-004, QD-003), `plan-BRIDGE-keyless-window-parent` (QD-184, as section 4 replaced it), `plan-BRIDGE-small-readings`, `plan-BRIDGE-windows-tun-driver` (QD-125), `g0-density-share-seal-format` (QD-108), `bridge-m2-01-egress-mode-field` (QD-630) and `bridge-m2-01-multi-use-approval` (QD-631). Section 4 stands as written: this section fills the compile its `Compile` step 4 calls and the engine its sink is, and changes neither.

### 12.1 The problem

§17.8 says in one sentence that "the compiler reads the config, verifies statements against §7.9's admissions and §8's grants, and compiles a `BridgeState` off the packet path", and in another that `device.Bridge` "applies it and later verified log entries, manages links, and swaps table and hook atomically". Four tasks build that: the compiler (BRIDGE-M4-16), the component around it with the host's NAT (BRIDGE-M4-17), shares (BRIDGE-M6-03) and their keys and signers (BRIDGE-M6-04). What has landed is the two ends: at the root, the statements' id-level rules and a body-level ledger (`BridgeLog`, `BridgeLedger`; BRIDGE-M2-01), and in `sidecar/device`, the posture, the egress policy and the disposition that turns one published state into the next (SDK-M4-01, BRIDGE-M4-06 to -14). Between them six things fail as written. Each is given as a run.

**A. Two readers, two ledgers.** A route's or a map's approval rides its sealed body (§17.8's `approval`), so api, which holds no config key, cannot judge it, and section 5's `tail_verdicts` carry no bit for it. The landed ledger judges it on S(n-1) through `ConfigState.StateAt`, which serves positions from the previous base to the tip and nothing a restored log never built, and answers `ErrBridgeApprovalUnverifiable`, void, for the rest.

1. Entry 40 is a `BridgeRoute` of 192.168.1.0/24 by host H, approved on Ana's phone. Entry 41 is a base.
2. Daemon D has followed the log since entry 30. It judged entry 40 at its position: the route is active, and D routes the prefix to H.
3. Phone P's VPN component restores its judge at base 41 for every compile (section 4.2.5). Entry 40 is below the base, where a restored log holds no state to judge it on: void. P answers the prefix unreachable.
4. H's own daemon restarts and restores at base 41. The route it advertises is void in its own state: rule 6 denies D's flows, which D's table sends.

The two ledgers then disagree on more than the one rule. The void route's `exposed_prefix` is free at P and held at D, so a `BridgeAlias` filed into it at entry 45 is valid at P and void at D, and one alias block routes to a foreign host on one device and nowhere on another. Nothing forks: both chain the same A_n. The landed code names the hole ("approvals older than the retained history are void unless the reader passes kept verdicts"), and kept verdicts are worse: they make the answer depend on how long a device has been running.

**B. A policy change turns a verdict for some readers only.** Entry 50 is a `BridgeMap` approved by Ben. Entry 52 is a base whose head removes Ben from the request rule's approvers and folds nothing. A reader present at 50 holds the verdict it judged then, active. A device that starts at base 52 can judge entry 50 only on base 52's rows, where Ben approves nothing: void. `BridgeFoldTwin-KeepOwnVerdict` reaches it, and `BridgeFoldTwin-NewDeviceVoid` reaches run A.

**C. A compile costs the network's history.** Rows carry nothing of the bridge but egress modes, because every other row would show a prefix, an address or a port (D-BRIDGE-6). So the only folded record of the bridge is the head's fold files, which hold every entry the log ever took (section 5.2.3). The landed design joins them ahead of the tail (`JoinBridgeLogs`) and opens every sealed body in log order, at every compile. A three-year-old team network with 400,000 entries has about 240 MB of fold files; the Apple extensions' compile is capped at 10 MiB (section 4.2.4), and a daemon would spend seconds of AEAD a compile to learn that nothing changed.

**D. The NAT keeps what the rules dropped.** D-BRIDGE-21 fences one flow against one revocation: register before the dial, publish before `CloseFlows`, recheck before the first byte. The engine around it has four more ways to lose a revocation.

1. *A late compile drops a denial.* `Bridge.Revoke(type, id, 0)` holds its narrowing "until the next state past the one in force". The state in force is at pin 60. A compile captures pin 61. Entry 62 is a `GrantRevoke` the root judged, and `Revoke` holds it at 61. The compile finishes: its state is at 61, "past the one in force", the narrowing is dropped, and the state, compiled before entry 62, admits the grant. `BridgeNatTwin-RevokeAtZero` is this run.
2. *A restart forgets the judge.* A daemon's root follower judges a `MemberRevoke` that two admins co-signed, which the posture cannot check on one signature, and narrows the bridge in memory. The process restarts before the next compile. The posture restores the last compiled state and the denials it could check; the provider starts; the revoked member's sidecar opens a flow. `BridgeNatTwin-ProviderBeforeCatchUp` is this run.
3. *A provider before its hook.* A new client generation builds a new NAT and provider. A Network source's first frame reaches the NAT before `SetEgressHook`: with no hook, connect's behavior is today's, and the flow opens to the host's LAN. Installing the hook cancels it, after its first bytes. `BridgeNatTwin-ProviderBeforeHook`.
4. *An address change resets the new address's flows.* Rule 3's tag is (subject, 3) for every hosted address, so when an old address's drain ends, `CloseFlows` ends every rule 3 flow of every subject, the ones opened to the new address included (question bridge-m4-11-rule-three-tags). D-BRIDGE-7 promises that an edit breaks no live TCP.

**E. Shares have formats in prose and a race in their keys.** §17.9 names a target table, an alias table, a ShareKey and a shortfall, each sealed under K, and QD-108 fixed the seal's bytes; no message has fields. Two more things are unsettled.

1. *A renewal races a removal.* Y's ShareKey holder read generation 7, certifies generation 7's signer for another 7 days, and writes it. Between its read and its write, Y removed sidecar R and rotated to generation 8. If the write lands in a head sealed at 7, R, which holds generation 7's key and is handed the ciphertext by the operator, reads a seed whose cert outlives R's removal by more than §17.9's 7 days. `ShareSignTwin-NoWriteGate` is this run.
2. *Two accepts take one block.* Two of Y's admins accept two shares at once. Each runs the preflight on the ledger it holds, and each takes the first free aligned block of the upper /17, the same one. Both `BridgeAlias` statements land. The ledger's rule gives the block to the first in log order and voids the second, whose share api then holds as `active` with an alias no router installs.

**F. Other clients, and where a signer's seed goes.** An sdk provider before C16 gives a sealed subject that no row binds `autogroup:untagged`'s rows, and `BridgeRules` has nowhere to put them, so under a document an app device loses the exit its policy grants (question bridge-m4-09-other-client-rows). And a share link built in an app's VPN component is signed there with the share's ShareSigner (§18.6's sign row), while §17.9 says the seed reaches "sidecar roles only, not `BridgeState`": the compile must hand the forwarding role a seed without putting it in the message that crosses the device RPC.

The requirement. Every reader that compiles at one pin holds one ledger: the same addresses, rules, aliases and verdicts, whatever base it started from and however long it has run. A compile reads a bounded amount, in one pass, with a working set that follows what reaches the host, on a daemon and in a VPN component by one code path. What the NAT carries is what the newest applied log position allows: no flow opens, and none stays open past its close, under a rule the device has durably judged revoked, across late compiles, timers, new client generations and restarts. A share's signer stops admitting a removed sidecar inside §17.9's bound, and nothing a renewal, a restart or a rotation does widens it.

### 12.2 The design

#### 12.2.1 The principle

Three rules, one for each of the compiler, the engine and the shares.

**One ledger, judged where the entry lands and frozen at the fold.** The *ledger* at a pin is what every sealed bridge body means there: who holds which address, which rules are active, void or withdrawn, each subject's egress spec, each alias. A body is judged on the state its entry lands on, by every reader that holds the body's generation, the rule BRIDGE-M2-01 already follows for whether a signer was an admin (`SignerAdmin`, "read on the state the entry lands on, so a base's re-application follows the rebuilt rows"). A base's tail is judged again as section 5 re-applies it, on the new base's rows. When a writer folds an entry it freezes the verdict it holds into the config head, as rows of the *ledger fold*, and every later reader takes the row. So a ledger is a function of the newest base's head and rows, the entries since its fold and the generation keys, and of nothing a reader remembers.

**One compile, a pure function, in passes.** `CompileBridgeState` maps (the state at a pin, the head that pin's base names, the unfolded bridge statements with their verdicts, the generation keys, the host's sidecar id, the host's local facts) to a `BridgeState`. It reads no clock, no network and no random source, iterates no Go map, and marshals deterministically, so two compilers given the same inputs return the same bytes. It reads the fold's files front to back a fixed number of times and keeps only what it was looking for, and it is the same code on a daemon and in a VPN component.

**One fence: persist, publish, close, and a gate at the start.** Every change of what a host enforces takes the same three steps in the same order: the evidence is durable, the policy is published at the next generation, and then the flows of every rule tag the new policy no longer admits are closed. A denial is held at its own log position, never at a relative one. After a start, the provider takes no frame until the hook is installed and every denial the device had judged before it stopped is applied again.

Shares add no fourth rule. A share's signer is a file in the config head, so the write gate that keeps a removed reader from reading new heads keeps it from new signers, and X's host holds a ratchet it never lowers.

#### 12.2.2 Formats settled

Each is additive. `config.proto` and `bridge.proto` are unfrozen until their milestones' gates (owner decision 194). Of these only `BridgeEgress.mode` is visible to a server, and QD-630 already ordered its §2.8 line. The ledger's files and the share grant are files of the config repo, which evs holds as ciphertext; the share tables and the alias body ride seals; and `BridgeRules` travels in process. So nothing here adds a §2.8 row.

```proto
// sidecar/protocol/config.proto: the bridge ledger's fold, files of the config head beside fold/<d>/<i>
message BridgeLedgerManifest {           // bridge/ledger/manifest
  uint32 format = 1;                     // 1
  uint64 folded_through = 2;             // the head's fold: the rows hold every bridge statement at or below it
  int64  time_ms = 3;                    // the time of the newest folded record: the fold's time, never a clock
  uint32 rule_shard_bits = 4;            // 8, or 16 from the fold at which the rows hold more than 262,144 rules
  repeated BridgeLedgerFile files = 5;   // every other ledger file the head holds, in path order
}
message BridgeLedgerFile { string path = 1; bytes sha256 = 2; uint64 row_count = 3; }

message BridgeLedgerAddresses { repeated BridgeLedgerAddressRow rows = 1; }    // bridge/ledger/addresses, by host_bits
message BridgeLedgerAddressRow {
  uint32 host_bits = 1;                  // the low 16 bits of the IPv4 (§17.4: kept across block changes)
  bytes  sidecar_id = 2;
  uint64 claimed_at = 3;                 // the BridgeAddress's entry
  uint64 released_at = 4;                // the entry that released it, its holder's revocation or removal; 0 live
  int64  released_ms = 5;                // that entry's time; the tombstone holds 30 days from it (I-14)
}

message BridgeLedgerRules { repeated BridgeLedgerRuleRow rows = 1; }           // bridge/ledger/rules/<xx>, by rule_id
message BridgeLedgerRuleRow {
  bytes  rule_id = 1;
  uint32 signed_type = 2;                // 0x1903 a route, 0x1904 a map
  bytes  owner = 3;                      // the advertiser or host, which signed the first filing
  uint64 first_at = 4;   int64 first_ms = 5;     // the first filing's entry and time
  uint64 newest_at = 6;  int64 newest_ms = 7;    // the newest filing of the held id
  BridgeLedgerDisposition disposition = 8;
  BridgeRouteBody route = 9;             // bridge.proto's: the body in force, its approval cleared: the first filing's,
  BridgeMapBody   map = 10;              //   with the newest filing's weight, site_id and drain_seconds; neither when void
  repeated bytes route_rule_ids = 11;
  int64  expires = 12;                   // a map's
  bool   standing = 13;                  // filed with no approval: active only where a standing grant covers it
  bytes  approval_id = 14;               // 16 B, with approval_not_after_ms and uses, when filed under a decision
  int64  approval_not_after_ms = 15;
  uint32 approval_uses = 16;             // the decision's budget, which counts every row that names approval_id
  uint64 withdrawn_at = 17;  int64 withdrawn_ms = 18;
  BridgeWithdrawMode withdraw_mode = 19;
  bytes  withdrawn_by = 20;              // the withdrawal's signer
  bool   withdrawn_by_admin = 21;
  int64  retain_until_ms = 22;           // when a withdrawn id leaves the rows; 0 keeps it for the network's life
}
enum BridgeLedgerDisposition {
  BRIDGE_LEDGER_DISPOSITION_UNSPECIFIED = 0;
  BRIDGE_LEDGER_DISPOSITION_ACTIVE = 1;      // the body is in force, subject to the compile's standing-grant check
  BRIDGE_LEDGER_DISPOSITION_VOID = 2;        // the body did not open or broke its rule: the id is held, nothing else
  BRIDGE_LEDGER_DISPOSITION_WITHDRAWN = 3;   // a BridgeWithdraw bound it; draining until withdrawn_ms + its drain
  BRIDGE_LEDGER_DISPOSITION_RESERVED = 4;    // a withdrawal ahead of the id's first filing: it binds withdrawn_by's
}                                            //   filings, or anyone's when withdrawn_by_admin

message BridgeLedgerEgressSpecs { repeated BridgeLedgerEgressRow rows = 1; }   // bridge/ledger/egress, by subject
message BridgeLedgerEgressRow {
  bytes  subject = 1;                    // a sidecar_id or a keyed atom
  BridgeEgressMode mode = 2;             // the newest BridgeEgress's clear mode (QD-630)
  repeated bytes exit_sidecar_ids = 3;   // under exits, from its body; none when the body is void
  bytes  exit_tag_id = 4;
  uint64 at = 5;
}

message BridgeLedgerAliases { repeated BridgeLedgerAliasRow rows = 1; }        // bridge/ledger/aliases, by
message BridgeLedgerAliasRow {                                                 //   (share_id, target_index)
  BridgeAliasBody body = 1;
  bytes  signer = 2;
  uint64 at = 3;
  uint64 released_at = 4;  int64 released_ms = 5;   // a release (below): draining until released_ms + its drain
}
```

```proto
// sidecar/protocol/bridge/bridge.proto
message BridgeApproval {
  // 1-2 as today
  bytes template_action = 3;             // QD-631 (owner decision 218)
}
message BridgeEgress {
  // 1-3 as today; BridgeEgressBody reserves 1
  BridgeEgressMode mode = 4;             // QD-630, once §2.8's api-7 names it
}
message BridgeAliasBody {
  // 1-4 as today
  bytes  host_identity_public_key = 5;   // QD-077: T_i's host's identity key, copied from the opened target table
  bytes  sharing_network_id = 6;         // X, the network the host is a sidecar of
  uint32 drain_seconds = 7;              // a release's drain, 300 s when 0, 3,600 s at most
  bool   release = 8;                    // ends the alias of this share_id and target_index; alias_prefix as held
}
message BridgeShareGrant {               // X's config file bridge/share-grant/<share_id hex> (QD-077)
  bytes  share_id = 1;
  bytes  grant_id = 2;                   // the share's GrantActivate; the file counts only while that grant is live
  bytes  share_public_key = 3;           // Y's ShareKey, Ed25519
  bytes  target_table_sha256 = 4;        // SHA-256 of the sealed target table as network_bridge_share stores it
  bytes  table_key = 5;                  // K
  bytes  accepting_network_id = 6;       // Y
  bytes  alias_table_sha256 = 7;         // SHA-256 of the sealed alias table X's approving admin opened
  uint64 target_table_version = 8;
  uint64 alias_table_version = 9;
}
// the share seal's bodies (QD-108): each sealed under K with its label, padded by pad to a multiple of 256 B
message BridgeShareTargets { repeated BridgeShareTarget targets = 1; bytes pad = 15; }      // label "targets"
message BridgeShareTarget {
  uint32 index = 1;                      // from 0, dense
  bytes  host_sidecar_id = 2;
  bytes  host_identity_public_key = 3;   // QD-077
  BridgeIpv4Prefix prefix = 4;           // what X's host reaches: its hosted address as a /32, or a served prefix
  uint32 protocol = 5;                   // 0 every protocol; 6 or 17 with ports
  repeated BridgePortRange ports = 6;
}
message BridgeShareAliases { repeated BridgeShareAlias aliases = 1; bytes pad = 15; }       // label "aliases"
message BridgeShareAlias {
  uint32 index = 1;
  uint32 alias_host_bits = 2;            // the low 16 bits of A_i's network address: Y's block is not X's to know
  uint32 length = 3;                     // equal to its target's
}
message BridgeShareKeyBody { bytes share_public_key = 1; bytes pad = 15; }                  // label "share-key"
message BridgeShareShortfall {                                                             // label "shortfall"
  uint32 index = 1;                      // the first target that found no room
  uint32 length = 2;                     // its prefix length
  uint32 free_address_count = 3;         // the upper /17's free addresses at the preflight
  uint32 largest_free_length = 4;        // the shortest prefix length with an aligned free block; 33 for none
  bytes  pad = 15;
}
message BridgeRules {
  // 1-9 as today
  BridgeRuleSubject untagged = 10;       // the rows autogroup:untagged holds at this host, with no sidecar_id,
                                         //   member_id or client_ids: what an sdk provider before C16 gives a
                                         //   sealed subject no row binds (bridge-m4-09-other-client-rows, option 1)
  repeated BridgeRuleShare shares = 11;  // the shares this host serves, X's side (17.9)
}
message BridgeRuleLink {
  // 1-9 as today
  bytes share_id = 10;                   // a share link, Y's side: FriendsAndFamily to an alias's host
  bytes target_network_id = 11;          // with share_id: X
}
message BridgeRuleShare {
  bytes share_id = 1;
  bytes accepting_network_id = 2;        // Y: the principal's network must be it
  bytes share_public_key = 3;            // as BridgeState.share_keys carries it
  bytes grant_id = 4;                    // a GrantRevoke of it ends the share between states
  int64 expires = 5;
  repeated BridgeRuleShareTarget targets = 6;   // the targets this host hosts, by index
}
message BridgeRuleShareTarget {
  uint32 index = 1;
  uint32 alias_host_bits = 2;
  uint32 length = 3;
  BridgeIpv4Prefix target = 4;           // T_i: To's low bits past length are kept
  uint32 protocol = 5;
  repeated BridgePortRange ports = 6;
}
```

**The head's paths** (`config_head.go`'s known paths gain them):

```text
bridge/ledger/manifest               one BridgeLedgerManifest; absent only in a head whose fold holds no bridge statement
bridge/ledger/addresses              BridgeLedgerAddresses; absent when it would hold no row, as every file below
bridge/ledger/egress                 BridgeLedgerEgressSpecs
bridge/ledger/aliases                BridgeLedgerAliases
bridge/ledger/rules/<xx>             BridgeLedgerRules whose rule_id begins with byte xx, two lowercase hex digits;
bridge/ledger/rules/<xx>/<yy>          with rule_shard_bits 16, by its first two bytes
bridge/share-grant/<share_id hex>    a BridgeShareGrant (QD-077), 32 hex digits
```

Encoding, which every writer on every leg must give alike, since the manifest hashes each file: protobuf's deterministic marshal; rows sorted by their key's bytes, `host_bits` as a number; no empty file; bodies carried as their messages with `approval` cleared and unknown fields refused, never as the bytes a signer sent; times as the log's `time_ms`. Rule ids are SHA-256 outputs or 32 random bytes, so rows spread evenly over the shards; the shard width is a function of the row count at the fold, so every writer picks the same one, and there is no cap on rules (owner decision 66).

**Rule tags.** `EgressDecision.RuleTag` stays the first 8 bytes of SHA-256(subject_id || rule_id). Rule 3's rule_id becomes five bytes, 0x03 and the hosted address's IPv4, so an old address's drain end closes that address's flows alone (bridge-m4-11-rule-three-tags, option 2); rules 4 and 7 keep their one byte. A share flow's subject_id is its `share_id` and its rule_id is five bytes, 0x53 and u32be(target index), since X's host cannot list Y's subjects. Every tag is still enumerable from the state without tracking flows.

**Settings.** `BridgeComponentSettings` (root; `DefaultBridgeComponentSettings()` fills them): `CompileDelay` 100 ms, `CompileMinInterval` 1 s, `CompileRetryInterval` 5 s doubling to 5 min, `CatchUpAlarmTimeout` 30 s, `WindowDelegationMaxLifetime` 168 h, `BindingRefreshInterval` 6 h, `BindingRetainTimeout` 7 days, `BindingMaxCount` 16 a subject, `ShareRenewInterval` 1 h, `ShareRenewBelow` 72 h, `ShareCertLifetime` 168 h, `ShareTableRefreshInterval` 1 h, `AcceptRetryCount` 3, `AutoAddressEnabled` false (plan-BRIDGE-small-readings #18). `BridgeLedgerSettings`: `ChunkByteCount` 64 KiB, `UnfoldedBodyMaxByteCount` 4 MiB (the opened bodies of the unfolded statements a compile holds; past it the compile refuses with `bridge_alarm` `ledger_over_budget` and the state stands), `RuleShardRowCount` 262,144. Amended 2026-11-12, QD-761: `BridgeLedgerSettings` gains `UnformedVoidWait` 24 h and `GenerationFormGrace` 1 h (12.2.3's void at the fold). Every reader of a network reads the grace's default, as it does the shard width, since a verdict rides on it; a wait below the grace plus 30 min is raised to that floor when the settings are read, so with the default grace the lowest wait is 90 min.

#### 12.2.3 The ledger: judging, the fold and its check

```text
JudgeBridgeBody(before, e at k)                  -- ConfigLogSettings.BridgeBodyJudge; nil at every keyless verifier
  the log calls it for each BridgeRoute and BridgeMap filing that takes effect: when it judges the entry, with
  before = S(k-1), and whenever it re-applies it at a base b, with before = R_b(k-1), b's rows with the tail's
  entries below k applied by their verdicts (section 5.2.3's Reapply)
  body := OpenConfigBody(e.sealed_body, keys)
     its generation is not held   -> Unopened{generation}
     its generation's GenRotate is signed more than GenerationFormGrace after e's time
                                  -> Refused{no such generation}: void, and no alarm (below; amended
                                     2026-11-12, QD-761)
     the seal or padding fails    -> Refused{seal}, which is the reader's alarm
  body.approval is unset          -> Standing        -- whether a standing grant covers it is the compile's (12.2.4)
  else  facts, err := before.CheckBridgeApproval(e, body, body.approval)   -- as landed, on `before` itself: action,
                                                        match, quorum and the spend check on before's AclState
        err -> Refused{err}  |  ok -> Approved{approval_id, rule_id, uses, not_after_ms}
  the verdict rides the BridgeLogStatement the state's fold then holds (Approval), as SignerAdmin does

OpenBridgeLedger(rows, unfolded, state, keys) -> ledger
  rows       T(ft), the head's ledger files, as 12.2.4's passes read them
  unfolded   state.Bridge(): the statements that took effect in (ft, n], in log order, each with its verdict
  for e in unfolded:
    BridgeAddress    the landed rules, over rows and the entries before e: the first claim in log order wins; a
                     second for an addressed host is void; a tombstone holds 30 days; the upper /17 only once the
                     lower is full, never inside an alias or an exposed prefix
    BridgeRoute,     Unopened -> pending: the id held, nothing active
    BridgeMap        Refused  -> void
                     Standing, Approved -> the landed rules: a held id changes only weight, site_id and
                       drain_seconds; a withdrawn or reserved id is void; D-BRIDGE-8; the body's shape; room for an
                       exposed prefix. Approved also: the statement's rule id is facts.rule_id, and the rows and
                       earlier entries that name facts.approval_id number fewer than facts.uses
    BridgeEgress     replaces its subject's spec; its exits from the body, none while pending or void
    BridgeAlias      void unless its signer was an admin's device where it landed (SignerAdmin). A release ends the
                     alias of its share_id and target_index, by that alias's signer or an admin, draining; any
                     other needs room in the upper /17 and a free (share_id, target_index)
    BridgeWithdraw   binds the rule it names, or reserves the id for its signer's filings (an admin's: anyone's)
  releases   a sidecar that state holds revoked at entry r, or whose member is gone, released its address at r
```

```text
a rule id's states in the ledger (a route or a map)
  none -> reserved             a BridgeWithdraw names the id before any filing
  none -> pending              its first filing took effect at id level and its body's generation is not held
  none, pending -> active      the body opens and passes its rules (Standing or Approved); in force only while
                               12.2.4's check holds at the state compiled
  none, pending -> void        the body does not open, breaks its rule, or its approval is Refused; or a fold
                               finds its generation unformed (below; amended 2026-11-12, QD-761)
  reserved -> void             a filing of the id by a signer the withdrawal binds
  active -> active             a filing of the held id: weight, site_id and drain_seconds only
  active -> withdrawn          a BridgeWithdraw by its owner or an admin: reset at once, or draining for
                               max(drain_seconds, 600 s)
  withdrawn, reserved -> none  the fold whose time passes retain_until_ms drops the row
  void -> void                 for the network's life
  unfolded -> frozen           a fold writes the row; pending is never frozen: a fold stops below it, or
                               freezes it void as unformed (amended 2026-11-12, QD-761)
```

`CheckBridgeApproval` changes in one way: it judges on its receiver, the state the log hands it, where the landed one asks `StateAt(statement.N - 1)`. `ErrBridgeApprovalUnverifiable` goes, and with it `BridgeLedgerReader.Approvals` and every verdict a reader kept for itself.

**Which state judges an unfolded filing.** For a reader at pin n whose newest base is b, with fold ft:

```text
k <= ft        the fold's row, frozen
ft < k < b     Judge(R_b(k-1), e_k): the tail, judged again at b on b's rows, as section 5 re-applies it
```
